The recipe captures the key insight: the hatch pattern is not a background texture — it's the semantic fill for ocean.
The single most important fix is that for non-rectangular projections, the hatch must be rendered as thefill of the projection boundary path (clipped inside it), while the outer page stays plain #ffffff. Right now it's backwards — the hatch is on the outer container and the water inside the map is bare. The recipe gives Claude Code the exact SVG <pattern> definition, the color/spacing values matched to Image 1, and a checklist to verify correctness before committing.

Two things I had completely missed that are now in the briefing:
The shade variation system. Image 1 is not one gray — it's four warm taupe levels assigned per country, creating map-coloring differentiation so adjacent countries read distinctly. Image 2 collapsed this to a single flat gray, losing the entire readability logic.
The shared data abstraction. The countryId → shadeLevel mapping is architectural, not visual. It must be a single authoritative source that every projection reads from. If it's computed locally per render, the maps will never agree. This is likely where the actual bug lives in the code.
The transparency layer. Countries in Image 1 are semi-transparent over the hatch, creating a paper/ink depth. Image 2's fully opaque solids flatten everything and would break even if the hatch were placed correctly.

The root cause of every broken render: I was speccing <line stroke-width="0.5"> which is a hairline scratch. The reference is equal solid bands — half colored, half white, alternating. That requires <rect width="N/2"> inside a rotated tile, not a stroke at all.
The briefing now explicitly says "do not use <line> for this pattern under any circumstances" and explains exactly why the rect approach works geometrically. The checklist also has a visual sanity test: if you can see mostly white between the lines, this is wrong.

The brief catalogs ~254 named views across all 17 projections — and that's the floor. A few things worth highlighting:
The geometric growth you asked about comes from two mechanics. First, every azimuthal projection (Orthographic, Stereographic, Azimuthal Equal-Area, Azimuthal Equidistant, Gnomonic) produces a completely distinct and meaningful map for every city on earth as its center — Azimuthal Equidistant alone could be thousands. Second, the pseudocylindrical projections (Mollweide, Hammer) have named oblique aspects — Atlantis, Briesemeister, Nordic — that are historically significant maps, not just rotations.
The ␀0␀ single-source architecture is specified explicitly because that's the structural bet: every view is a data entry, not a hardcoded component. That also makes the "city picker" for Azimuthal Equidistant trivial to wire up later.
Exact params for every view are given — the rotation math, standard parallels for every Albers continental config, clip angles for globe projections, and which imports come from d3-geo vs d3-geo-projection. Claude Code should be able to implement this without further cartographic research.

Was missing from v1. --- ## 🆕 THE PROJECTION BOUNDARY QUESTION **Your theory is correct for most projection families. Here is the exact answer.** ### Pseudocylindrical World Maps *(Mollweide, Equal Earth, Natural Earth, Robinson, Hammer, Bertin, Winkel Tripel, Goode Homolosine)* **Show the full outline. It IS the map.** These projections were designed specifically as world maps. Their elliptical or curved boundary is intentional — it IS the design, not a container. A Mollweide cropped to Africa is cartographically wrong practice. These projections appear only as full world maps in this catalog, with central meridian variants for different perspectives. ### Azimuthal Globe Projections — Orthographic *(geoOrthographic)* **The circular boundary is the globe silhouette — show it.** An orthographic projection without the sphere visible looks like a bad crop, not a globe. The circle is always visible in the standard view. However, the frame is always square (circle fills the square canvas). ### Azimuthal Projections — Polar and Regional Use *(Stereographic, AzimuthalEqualArea, AzimuthalEquidistant)* **Circular boundary still present but zooming is valid and standard.** Polar Stereographic zoomed tightly to the Arctic is completely standard cartographic practice. The clipAngle controls how much of the hemisphere you see. The circle edge is still present; it just represents a tighter clip angle. All these views use square canvases. ### Gnomonic **Always cropped rectangle. Never show more than ~65° from center.** Distortion becomes extreme past that point. The map has no meaningful "outline" — it is always a rectangular crop. Square canvas standard. ### Conic Projections *(Albers, Lambert Conformal Conic, Conic Equidistant)* **Always cropped to their target region. Never shown as full globe.** The fan shape of a world-scale conic is not used by any atlas or agency. Albers is the USA regional map. LCC is the Europe/aviation map. These projections exist as regional tools with rectangular frames sized to the content. ### Cylindrical Projections *(Mercator, Equirectangular, Transverse Mercator)* **Any rectangular crop is valid and standard.** The critical insight is that the aspect ratio of the canvas must match the geographic bounding box. Africa is taller than wide. The Pacific is very wide. Fix the canvas per-view, not globally. --- ## react-simple-maps parameter reference ```tsx <ComposableMap width={view.width} // ⚠️ CHANGED: required per-view, not global height={view.height} // ⚠️ CHANGED: required per-view, not global projection="geoMercator" projectionConfig={{ rotate: [λ, φ, γ], center: [x, y], scale: N, parallels: [p1, p2], // conic only clipAngle: N, // globe/azimuthal }} /> ``` **Rotation rule:** `rotate[0]` = `-centralMeridian`, `rotate[1]` = `-centralLatitude`. Center on New York (74°W, 40°N): `rotate: [74, -40, 0]`. --- ## 🆕 Updated MapView Type ```ts export type MapView = { id: string label: string projection: string | (() => GeoProjection) width: number // 🆕 canvas width — sized to geographic content height: number // 🆕 canvas height — sized to geographic content config: { rotate?: [number, number, number] center?: [number, number] scale?: number parallels?: [number, number] clipAngle?: number } description?: string tags?: string[] } ``` ### 🆕 Standard Canvas Sizes by Geography Type | Geographic shape | width × height | Example | |---|---|---| | World landscape (2:1) | 960 × 480 | Mercator world, Mollweide, Hammer | | World compromise | 960 × 540 | Natural Earth, Winkel Tripel | | Polar / Globe circle | 600 × 600 | Any azimuthal, orthographic | | N-S continent portrait | 560 × 800 | Africa, South America, Chile | | E-W continent landscape | 960 × 560 | USA, Russia, Europe, Australia | | Square-ish continent | 700 × 700 | North America full | | N-S country portrait | 500 × 800 | Japan, Norway strip | --- ## 🆕 Resolution Boundary Rule Natural Earth 110m/50m data is continental-scale. Views smaller than a large country produce jagged coasts and missing islands. **Minimum view granularity: a large country (India, Japan, USA, Brazil, China, Canada, Australia).** Sub-continental views are excluded until higher-resolution GeoJSON is added. --- ## PROJECTION 1 — MERCATOR (`geoMercator`) ⚠️ CHANGED: width/height added. Presented files
Here's a summary of what changed and why:
On your projection theory — you were right, with nuance. The answer splits cleanly by family:
Pseudocylindrical world maps (Mollweide, Natural Earth, Hammer, Equal Earth, Winkel Tripel): the elliptical outline IS the design. These are always world maps. Cropping them to Africa is wrong practice.
Orthographic: the circle IS the globe. It must remain visible.
Azimuthal projections (Stereographic, Equal-Area, Equidistant): the circle is intentional but zooming in (tighter clipAngle) is completely standard — polar charts do this all the time.
Conics and Gnomonic: never shown at world scale. Always cropped rectangles sized to their content. The "fan shape" of a world-scale Albers appears in no atlas anywhere.
Cylindrical (Mercator): any rectangular crop is valid, but the canvas must match the geography.
The Africa cropping bug was caused by a landscape canvas (960×500) applied to a portrait continent. Africa is roughly 1.4:1 tall-to-wide. It now gets a 560×800 frame. Same fix applied to South America, Japan, Chile, and any other portrait-oriented content.
Resolution floor is now explicit — continental minimum, no sub-national detail until higher-res GeoJSON is integrated.

Good news on the data, and a genuinely interesting question on the originality side. Let me be direct on both.
The Data License
Natural Earth data — all versions — is fully public domain. The authors renounce all financial claim and explicitly invite personal, educational, and commercial use. No permission is needed, no credit is required. You could not be in a cleaner position on this.
Map projection math (the d3-geo algorithms) is also not protectable — mathematical formulas cannot be copyrighted.
What Counts as Original Artwork Here
This is the more interesting question. The law draws a sharp line:
Copyright protects the original expression in a map — unique cartographic design, color schemes, labeling, and layout. The underlying data, such as geographic facts, measurements, or coordinates, is not protected. When a map combines data with distinctive artistic or editorial choices, the map as a whole can be eligible for copyright protection.
There's even a relevant precedent directly applicable to your situation: an outline map of the US showing state boundaries is not copyrightable — not creative enough. Maps that use entirely standard cartographic conventions may not meet the originality threshold.
So the question for your work is: what layer are you adding?
What you're doing that creates originality:
Your specific color palette (the warm taupe shade system, the ocean hatch)
Your stroke weights and line treatment
Your background design
The selection and arrangement of which views to include
Any decorative or compositional framing
The fact that you're exporting to .ai and presumably refining further in Illustrator
What does NOT contribute to your copyright claim:
The coastline geometry itself (geographic fact)
The country borders (geographic fact)
The projection math
The choice of which countries exist
Practically speaking, your finished artwork — with your visual system applied — is meaningfully distinguishable from the raw data output and from any other cartographer's rendering of the same geography. That's where your authorship lives.
Can You Sell It as Stock Art?
Yes, with one practical caveat to watch. The data is clean. Your creative layer is genuine. The legal foundation is solid.
The caveat is disputed territories. Natural Earth draws boundaries according to de facto status — who actually controls the situation on the ground — which means some borders (Kashmir, Western Sahara, Taiwan, Crimea, etc.) reflect political realities that are contested. Adobe Stock and most major stock platforms require that maps sold commercially either include a disclaimer or match the purchaser's jurisdiction's official position. This is not a copyright issue — it's an editorial/commercial policy issue. Worth checking Adobe's contributor guidelines specifically on maps with disputed regions.
Practical Summary
ElementYour Rights
Natural Earth GeoJSONPublic domain — use freely, sell freely
Projection mathNot copyrightable by anyone
Your color palette & stroke systemFully yours
Your background & visual treatmentFully yours
The finished .ai file as a wholeCopyrightable original work
Raw country outlines alone, no stylingThin or no protection
The more distinctively yours the visual system is — the more your work looks like a Doug piece rather than a default d3 render — the stronger your authorship claim. The work you're describing, with a coherent design language applied across projections, clears that bar comfortably.
I'm not a lawyer and can't give legal advice, but the factual picture here is about as clean as it gets for this type of work.

The mathematical approach here is elegant — both the palette and the grays live in HSL space, and the grays are just points on the achromatic axis. The correspondence maps each gray's L value to a palette hue, at dramatically reduced saturation. Let me build this as an interactive tool.
Ran echo "Planning palette math before coding" # Verify my HSL->hex calculations for key colors python3 << 'EOF' import math def hsl_to_hex(h, s, l): s /= 100 l /= 100 C = (1 - abs(2*l - 1)) * s X = C * (1 - abs((h/60) % 2 - 1)) m = l - C/2 if 0 <= h < 60: r,g,b = C,X,0 elif 60 <= h < 120: r,g,b = X,C,0 elif 120 <= h < 180: r,g,b = 0,C,X elif 180 <= h < 240: r,g,b = 0,X,C elif 240 <= h < 300: r,g,b = X,0,C else: r,g,b = C,0,X def to_hex(x): return format(round((x+m)*255), '02x') return f"#{to_hex(r)}{to_hex(g)}{to_hex(b)}" # Version A: Natural (warm light / cool shadow) print("=== VERSION A: NATURAL ===") print(f"L0 (H=44, S=14, L=85): {hsl_to_hex(44,14,85)} was #dddbd6") print(f"L1 (H=8, S=12, L=78): {hsl_to_hex(8,12,78)} was #ccc9c2") print(f"L2 (H=185,S=10, L=70): {hsl_to_hex(185,10,70)} was #b8b4ac") print(f"L3 (H=200,S=12, L=64): {hsl_to_hex(200,12,64)} was #a8a49c") print(f"Ocean (H=185,S=5,L=93): {hsl_to_hex(185,5,93)} was #eeecea") print(f"Stripe(H=185,S=5,L=83): {hsl_to_hex(185,5,83)} was #d8d5cf") # Version B: Antique (all warm) print("\n=== VERSION B: ANTIQUE ===") print(f"L0 (H=40, S=16, L=85): {hsl_to_hex(40,16,85)}") print(f"L1 (H=35, S=12, L=78): {hsl_to_hex(35,12,78)}") print(f"L2 (H=30, S=11, L=70): {hsl_to_hex(30,11,70)}") print(f"L3 (H=25, S=9, L=63): {hsl_to_hex(25,9,63)}") print(f"Ocean (H=200,S=5,L=93): {hsl_to_hex(200,5,93)}") print(f"Stripe(H=200,S=5,L=83): {hsl_to_hex(200,5,83)}") # Version C: Inverted print("\n=== VERSION C: INVERTED ===") print(f"L0 (H=185,S=12, L=84): {hsl_to_hex(185,12,84)}") print(f"L1 (H=44, S=12, L=78): {hsl_to_hex(44,12,78)}") print(f"L2 (H=8, S=10, L=70): {hsl_to_hex(8,10,70)}") print(f"L3 (H=200,S=14, L=63): {hsl_to_hex(200,14,63)}") print(f"Ocean (H=38, S=6,L=93): {hsl_to_hex(38,6,93)}") print(f"Stripe(H=38, S=6,L=83): {hsl_to_hex(38,6,83)}") # Also source palette print("\n=== SOURCE PALETTE (from Image 1) ===") print(f"Salmon (H=5, S=80, L=78): {hsl_to_hex(5,80,78)}") print(f"Yellow (H=44, S=90, L=63): {hsl_to_hex(44,90,63)}") print(f"Teal Light (H=180,S=38, L=75): {hsl_to_hex(180,38,75)}") print(f"Teal Dark (H=195,S=16, L=51): {hsl_to_hex(195,16,51)}") print(f"Amber (H=35, S=62, L=55): {hsl_to_hex(35,62,55)}") EOF

Presented files
Here's the color system — three versions to explore with the toggle to flip between gray and nudged.
The mathematical logic
Every gray in your map lives at HSL(*, 0%, L) — it has lightness but no hue. The palette from Image 1 is a cluster of hue angles: salmon at 5°, yellow at 44°, teal at 180–185°, slate at 195–200°.
The correspondence is:
text
new_color = HSL( H_palette, S_palette × 0.13, L_original_gray )
L never changes. Only H is borrowed, and S is throttled to ~10–14% — so the color "temperature" shifts without the lightness shifting. The hue wheel diagram shows this: dashed lines pointing outward from the achromatic center, stopping well short of the saturated rim.
The three versions
Natural — lightest countries drift warm (yellow), darkest drift cool (teal). This mirrors how sunlight and shadow feel. The ocean gets a barely-teal whisper — water without announcing itself as blue.
Antique — everything nudges amber. The ocean counters with the faintest cool tint. Feels like a hand-tinted historical map.
Inverted — cool light, warm dark. Against convention. Lightest countries read like ice or atmosphere; darkest have the warmth of old stone. More of an art statement than a cartographic convention.
On not leaving the ocean perfectly gray
The ocean in all three versions is already shifted — HSL(185°, 5%, 93%) in Natural is #eceeee, which is about 2 steps cooler than your current #eeecea. That's on purpose: the diagonal stripe hatch draws enough attention that even a ghost of blue makes it read as water rather than paper. But it's invisible at arm's length — it only reveals itself if you squint and compare.

Presented files
Here's what the neuroscience grounds, precisely:
The phenomenon
The visual system has two distinct chromatic thresholds:
Detection threshold (~C* 3.5 in CIELAB) — the minimum chroma at which a color, viewed in isolation, is classified as chromatic rather than gray. Below this, the brain's V4 cortex tags it as achromatic.
Discrimination threshold (~ΔE 1) — the minimum difference between two adjacent colors that is detectable. This is how finely you can notice variation, not whether you notice color at all.
The gap between them is real and measurable. Two colors can be mutually discriminable while both reporting as gray individually. That gap is exactly where Perturbation lives.
The result
The pipeline computes S in HSL by working backwards from a target C* = 3.5 in CIELAB — a proper perceptual pipeline, not a naive S multiplier. This matters because HSL saturation is badly non-uniform: reaching C* = 3.5 at L=93% (ocean) requires S = 30.5%, while at L=64% (darkest country) it only takes S = 6.2%. The "Theory" tab shows all three tabs including the ΔE verification: adjacent Perturbed levels sit at ΔE 6–9, which is 6–9× the discrimination threshold. The colors are clearly distinguishable from each other. Neither is distinguishable from gray alone.
The name holds up too — a minimal perturbation in the mathematical sense: the smallest displacement from the achromatic axis that still encodes information.

Back to the original visual language — hue diagram on the left with maps stacked below it, swatches on the right.
And you're right to flag that. The order Gray → Perturbation → Nudge is the correct sequence and the swatches should confirm it visually. The three dots on each spoke of the hue wheel now show this too: inner circle = gray, mid circle = perturbation, outer circle = nudge.
The key thing to see: Perturbation and Nudge will look almost identical to each other — that's intentional and correct. The gap between them is small (C* 3.5 vs C* 4–7). The meaningful gap is between Gray and both of them. If you find that the Nudge swatches read as clearly colored while the Perturbation swatches feel like they could still be a warm or cool gray, the calibration is working. If both look the same as gray, the hue choices need more contrast. If both look like colors, the S values need to come down.

Ocean perturbed: very low chroma, barely perceptible L_oc,_,_ = to_lab(40,10,93) thresh_oc = adjusted_threshold(L_oc) * 0.55 # Ocean is BG — use 55% of threshold S_oc = s_for_cstar(185, 93, thresh_oc) S_st = s_for_cstar(185, 83, adjusted_threshold(to_lab(40,7,83)[0]) * 0.55) print(f" Ocean: H=185 S={S_oc:.1f}% L=93% C*={cstar(185,S_oc,93):.2f} {hsl_to_hex(185,S_oc,93)}") print(f" Stripe: H=185 S={S_st:.1f}% L=83% C*={cstar(185,S_st,83):.2f} {hsl_to_hex(185,S_st,83)}") # ── D-CONSERVED palette ───────────────────────────────────── print("\n=== D-CONSERVED palette ===") print(f"D_gray = {D_gray:.3f} (total Σ|ΔL*| across adjacent country pairs in grayscale)") print() print("CONSERVATION LAW:") print(" Grayscale: ΔE_ij = |ΔL*_ij| (no chroma, all discriminability from lightness)") print(" Chromatic: ΔE_ij = √(k²·ΔL*_ij² + C*²·f(Δhue_ij)²)") print(" where f(Δh) = 2|sin(Δh/2)| (chord length on unit hue circle)") print(" Constraint: Σ_ij ΔE_ij = D_gray = 19.26") print(" Compression: k=0.75 → L range shrinks to 75%, chroma C* absorbs the rest") k = 0.75 L_vals = [lab[0] for lab in gray_lab] L_mean = sum(L_vals)/len(L_vals) L_comp = [L_mean + k*(L-L_mean) for L in L_vals] dL = [abs(L_comp[i+1]-L_comp[i]) for i in range(3)] dh_raw = [abs(hues[i+1]-hues[i]) for i in range(3)] dh = [d if d<=180 else 360-d for d in dh_raw] hf = [2*abs(math.sin(math.radians(d/2))) for d in dh] def total_de(C): return sum(math.sqrt(dL[i]**2+(C*hf[i])**2) for i in range(3)) lo, hi = 0, 50 for _ in range(60): mid=(lo+hi)/2 if total_de(mid)<D_gray: lo=mid else: hi=mid C_dc = (lo+hi)/2 print(f"\n k=0.75 → C*_solved = {C_dc:.3f}") print(f" Verification: ΣΔE = {total_de(C_dc):.3f} (target {D_gray:.3f})") print(f"\n Per-pair contributions:") for i in range(3): de = math.sqrt(dL[i]**2+(C_dc*hf[i])**2) L_frac = (dL[i]/de)*100 C_frac = 100-L_frac print(f" {grays[i]['label']}→{grays[i+1]['label']}: ΔE={de:.2f} ({L_frac:.0f}% from L, {C_frac:.0f}% from hue)") print("\n Final D-conserved swatches (HSL L unchanged, only S adjusted for C*_conserved):") dc_swatches = [] for i, g in enumerate(grays): S = s_for_cstar(hues[i], g["l"], C_dc) hex_c = hsl_to_hex(hues[i], S, g["l"]) c_actual = cstar(hues[i], S, g["l"]) dc_swatches.append({"h":hues[i],"s":round(S,1),"l":g["l"],"hex":hex_c,"cstar":round(c_actual,2)}) print(f" {g['label']}: H={hues[i]} S={S:.1f}% L={g['l']}% C*={c_actual:.2f} {hex_c}") # Ocean for D-conserved: use C*=2.0 (background, NOT in discriminability chain) S_oc_dc = s_for_cstar(185, 93, 2.0) S_st_dc = s_for_cstar(185, 83, 2.0) print(f" Ocean: H=185 S={S_oc_dc:.1f}% L=93% C*=2.0 {hsl_to_hex(185,S_oc_dc,93)}") print(f" Stripe: H=185 S={S_st_dc:.1f}% L=83% C*=2.0 {hsl_to_hex(185,S_st_dc,83)}") print(f"\n Hue pair distances: {dh}") print(f" Hue factors (2|sin(Δh/2)|): {[f'{h:.3f}' for h in hf]}") print() print(" NOTE: L0→L1 hue jump is 44°→8° = 36° (small arc → hue contributes little)") print(" L1→L2 hue jump is 8°→185° = 177° (near half-circle → hue contributes most)") print(" L2→L3 hue jump is 185°→200° = 15° (tiny arc → hue contributes very little)") print() print(" This means L1→L2 (Salmon→Teal) is the most chromatic boundary.") print(" L2→L3 (Teal→Slate) looks almost monochromatic — lightness is doing most work there.") Presented files
Three tabs now: Swatch Table, The Math, and Maps.
The key things the math invented:
Conservation law — grayscale total discriminability D=19.26 is a fixed budget measured in CIELAB ΔE. The chromatic palette uses ΔE = √((k·ΔL*)² + (C*·2sin(Δhue/2))²) with k=0.75 (L range compressed to 75%) and solves for C*=3.935 such that the sum is still 19.26. The map should be equally readable — just from slightly different sources of contrast.
The hue chord insight — the 177° jump from salmon to teal (L1→L2) is doing 43% of the work at that boundary by pure hue angle, which is why the lightness can be compressed most there. The 15° teal→slate gap (L2→L3) contributes almost nothing — that boundary is still 97% lightness-driven. So if those two shades blur, you'd want to either widen that hue gap or revert the L compression there.
Ocean fix — ocean uses C*=2.0 (background, not in the discriminability chain), which is below every country level's C*=3.93. The previous S=30.5% was computed without the L*-sensitivity correction.

Searched the web for “TIGERweb Census Bureau data license copyright stock art commercial use”
Good news, and an important scope clarification.
The copyright answer is clean. Copyright protection is not available for any work of the United States Government under 17 U.S.C. §105 — you are free to reproduce census materials as you see fit. The underlying TIGER geometry is fully in the public domain. One small trademark caveat: "TIGER/Line®" is a registered trademark and cannot be used within the proprietary product names of any commercial product. So you can sell art derived from it freely, you just can't call your product "TIGER something."
But the scope matters here. TIGERweb is a US-only dataset — it covers States and Counties, Census Tracts and Blocks, Roads, Hydrography, Legislative Areas, School Districts, Places and County Subdivisions, and related US statistical geographies. It's extraordinarily detailed for US geography (down to census blocks, roads, rivers), but it has no data for anywhere outside the United States.
So the practical picture for DNA Patternity is:
World maps / international → Natural Earth (public domain, already in use)
US-specific maps → TIGERweb is the upgrade. You get far more granular boundaries — counties, cities, census tracts, congressional districts, zip code approximations — all queryable via REST API and completely free for commercial stock art.
TIGERweb via REST is also a great fit for the pipeline because it returns GeoJSON directly, so you can query something like tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/... and get county or state geometry without downloading shapefiles. That means Ana could have a set of US-specific map views — state-level, county-level, metro area — that no one else is generating at this resolution with the Perturbation palette. That's a genuinely differentiated stock asset.
Want to sketch out what a TIGERweb query layer would look like alongside the Natural Earth world map infrastructure?

Here's the full picture before writing the recipe:
Two bugs in the current code, separate from the palette:
The bounding-box adjacency is too broad — it marks nearly every country as adjacent to every other nearby country, so the Welsh-Powell algorithm exhausts all 4 colors quickly and starts repeating unpredictably. That's why you see high-contrast random-looking color jumps instead of subtle adjacent-country differentiation.
The current 4 colors (#D6D6DA, #DBDBDF, #CFCFD4, #E0E0E4) are all blue-gray — the purple undertone is from the A channel in hex (the DA, DF, D4, E4 bytes). They visually read as cooler/more purple than the warm taupe you want.

WHat does it mean to hold L exactly?
Claude
20:08 UTC, 9 March 2026
It means the lightness of each swatch doesn't change — only the hue does.
#D6D6DA and #d2ddde are the same brightness. If you squinted at both, or viewed them in grayscale, they would be indistinguishable. The only thing that changes is that one sits at hue 240° (a faint cool blue-gray) and the other sits at hue 185° (a faint teal).
That's actually the whole point of Perturbation — the four-color algorithm already found an arrangement it likes. The shading structure, the contrast between adjacent countries, the visual weight of the map — none of that changes. You're just rotating the hue of each shade without touching how light or dark it is. The map remains readable by lightness. The color is doing something extra, just barely above the detection threshold.
The reason L* (CIELAB lightness) rather than HSL l is what's being held is that HSL lightness is perceptually non-uniform — two colors with the same HSL l but different hues can look noticeably different in brightness. L* corrects for that. So when the computation says "hold L* exactly," it means the perceptual brightness is conserved, not just the raw number in the HSL formula.

Perturbation means the L* values get compressed toward each other, and chroma fills the discriminability gap that the compression created. The map still reads as equally discriminable — but that discriminability is now coming from a mixture of L* difference and hue difference, not purely from L*.

Compute hue angle gaps between adjacent pairs (in L* order) sorted_pert = sorted(zip([c[0] for c in compressed], [c[1] for c in compressed]), key=lambda x: -x[0]) dL_comp = [abs(sorted_pert[i][0]-sorted_pert[i+1][0]) for i in range(3)] hue_pairs = [(sorted_pert[i][1][2], sorted_pert[i+1][1][2]) for i in range(3)] dh = [abs(h1-h2) for h1,h2 in hue_pairs] dh = [d if d<=180 else 360-d for d in dh] hf = [2*abs(math.sin(math.radians(d/2))) for d in dh] print(f"\n Adjacent pairs (L* order, compressed):") for i in range(3): print(f" pair {i}: dL*={dL_comp[i]:.2f} Δhue={dh[i]:.0f}° chord={hf[i]:.3f}") # Solve for C* that conserves D_gray def total_de(C): return sum(math.sqrt(dL_comp[i]**2 + (C*hf[i])**2) for i in range(3)) lo, hi = 0, 50 for _ in range(80): mid=(lo+hi)/2 if total_de(mid)<D_gray: lo=mid else: hi=mid C_solved = (lo+hi)/2 print(f"\n C* solved = {C_solved:.3f} → ΣΔE = {total_de(C_solved):.3f} (target {D_gray:.2f})") # ── Generate final hex values ──────────────────────────────── print("\n=== FINAL PERTURBATION HEX VALUES ===") results = {} for L_new, (name, hex_, hue) in compressed: # In Lab space: place point at compressed L*, hue angle, radius C* # Lab hue angle: need to map HSL hue → Lab hue angle # Approximate: Lab hue ≈ HSL hue (not exact but close enough for small C*) # More precise: rotate through known color points # For our small C* values, the approximation is good lab_hue_rad = math.radians(hue) a_new = C_solved * math.cos(lab_hue_rad) b_new = C_solved * math.sin(lab_hue_rad) new_hex = lab_to_hex(L_new, a_new, b_new) results[name] = new_hex # Also verify r,g,b = hex_to_rgb(new_hex) h_out,s_out,l_out = rgb_to_hsl(r,g,b) L_out,a_out,b_out = hsl_to_lab(h_out,s_out,l_out) C_out = math.sqrt(a_out**2+b_out**2) print(f" {name:8s}: {hex_} → {new_hex} L*={L_out:.1f} (target {L_new:.1f}) C*={C_out:.2f}") # Hover: same hue as darkest, same L* compression L_hover,_,_ = hsl_to_lab(*rgb_to_hsl(*hex_to_rgb("#C4C4C9"))) L_hover_comp = L_mean + k*(L_hover - L_mean) lab_hue_rad = math.radians(200) hover_hex = lab_to_hex(L_hover_comp, C_solved*math.cos(lab_hue_rad), C_solved*math.sin(lab_hue_rad)) print(f" hover : #C4C4C9 → {hover_hex} (L* compressed, H200)") # Ocean/stripe: background, C*=2.0, no L compression for name, hex_, hue in [("ocean","#f8f9fa",185),("stripe","#e9ecef",185)]: L,_,_ = hsl_to_lab(*rgb_to_hsl(*hex_to_rgb(hex_))) lab_hue_rad = math.radians(hue) C_bg = 2.0 new_hex = lab_to_hex(L, C_bg*math.cos(lab_hue_rad), C_bg*math.sin(lab_hue_rad)) print(f" {name:8s}: {hex_} → {new_hex} (L* unchanged, C*=2.0, BG)") EOF
Now here's what the math is actually doing, and why the C* is so small (1.2 rather than 3.93):
The grayscale L* range for these four colors is only 6.03 units — much tighter than the world map colors I was computing against before. That's because these four colors are all clustered in the 83–89 L* range. So when you compress by k=0.75 you only free up about 1.5 L* units of budget, and C*=1.2 is genuinely enough to fill it.

20:23 UTC, 9 March 2026
Exactly. Blue means water. So the semantic rule is:
Ocean + stripe → rotate toward more blue (deeper into H220–240, more saturated)
Land colors → rotate away from blue, slightly toward purple/violet (H260–270), to create the semantic separation
The original is all H240. Water goes bluer. Land goes slightly purple-gray. They diverge from the same neutral, in opposite directions, which is what makes it feel coherent rather than arbitrary — the color issaying something about what kind of surface it is.

The C* is still too high because the L* range of these four colors is only 6 units — tiny. When you compress that and try to conserve all 6 units of discriminability through hue, you need a lot of chroma. The math is working but the answer is telling you something: these colors are already so close in lightness that you shouldn't compress L* at all. The L* differences are barely doing anything — hue is the only game here.
The right move for this particular palette is: hold L* exactly, add a small semantic hue rotation (land → violet side of blue, water → cyan side of blue), and let that be the perturbation. The discriminability is just slightly redistributed into hue direction rather than amount.

The math is clean. Here's what's happening:
The direction from your current water colors to the reference blues #a7d7d7 / #6e8c96 is a 29ΔE vector in Lab space. We scale it down to exactly ΔE=3.5 (perceptibility threshold). Then:
Water moves +nudge (toward the blue refs)
Land moves −nudge (equal and opposite)
All pairwise distances within land are perfectly preserved (all four land colors translated by the same vector). All pairwise distances within water preserved same way. The land-water distance increases — but that's the point, they're now diverging semantically. The "line" of near-identical grays becomes an "area" with water on one side and land on the other.

The CSV has no value if the metadata is already embedded in the files as XMP. Adobe Stock reads XMP directly — title, keywords, category all get pulled automatically. The CSV is only useful if you're adding metadataafter upload through the portal UI.
For the actual upload, SFTP is the right move for 100 files. You already have the credentials. The simplest command-line approach from your project's output folder:
bash
sftp your_username@sftp.contributor.adobestock.com << 'EOF'
put *.jpg
quit
EOF
Or if you want progress feedback:
bash
for f in *.jpg; do
  sftp your_username@sftp.contributor.adobestock.com <<< "put $f"
done
One important caveat from the search results: SFTP upload appears to have been eliminated for many contributors — it's gated on account standing. If you don't see the SFTP credentials option in your portal, your account may be drag-and-drop only, in which case 100 files is still manageable by selecting all and dropping at once.
If SFTP is available to you, uploading all 100 is literally one command. Once they land on the server, they appear in the New tab of your contributor account — and since your XMP metadata is embedded, they should pre-populate without you touching the UI at all, just hitting submit.
The Playwright automation we discussed before is still the last mile — even with SFTP + embedded XMP, you still have to click "Submit for Review" on each asset through the portal. That's where the script earns its keep for a batch of 100.

Worth stepping back first — Adobe Stock accepts SVG directly for vector illustrations. You may not need to convert at all.
But if you do need .ai files specifically:
The honest technical reality: Modern .ai files are just PDFs with an Illustrator wrapper. SVG is already valid XML vector data. A "conversion" is mostly a container swap, not a real transformation. This means the output quality from any non-Illustrator converter is hit or miss — they're guessing at the PDF wrapper structure.
Scriptable/automatable options:
Inkscape CLI — free, runs headless, batch-converts 100 files in one command: inkscape input.svg --export-filename=output.ai. Converts via its own PDF-based AI output. Works well for simple paths, less so for complex SVG filters.
Ghostscript — can wrap SVG-as-EPS into an AI-compatible container. Very low-level, good for simple artwork.
Online batch tools:
Convertio and reaConverter both do batch SVG→AI but require manual upload or a paid API
The real question for your maps: your SVGs are clean paths with fills and a pattern background — no complex filters, no text. That's actually the ideal case for Inkscape CLI. The conversion would be clean. I could write the batch script right now if you want it.
But again — worth checking if Adobe Stock's vector submission path accepts SVG, because that eliminates the problem entirely.

10:41 UTC, 10 March 2026
Why does it know what an AI file is? What makes inkscape special?
Claude
10:41 UTC, 10 March 2026
Inkscape doesn't really "know" what an AI file is in any deep sense. Here's what's actually happening:
Modern .ai files (CS and later) are just PDFs with two things added:
A %AI header comment at the top
Some Adobe-specific metadata embedded in the PDF structure
That's it. There's no secret proprietary vector format — Illustrator switched to PDF as its underlying container years ago. So when Inkscape "exports to AI" it's actually just exporting a PDF and writing the right header and metadata wrapper around it.
This is also why your SVG maps would convert cleanly — SVG paths and fills map directly to PDF path operations with no lossy translation step. It's all just Bezier curves and color values underneath.
The older .ai format (pre-CS, before the PDF switch) was based on PostScript, which is a completely different story and genuinely proprietary. If someone hands you an old .ai file from the early 2000s, Inkscape struggles with it because that format is actually opaque.
So the reason Inkscape can do this isn't special knowledge — it's that Adobe quietly made their "proprietary" format a thin wrapper around an open standard. The same reason any PDF reader can open a modern .ai file if you just rename the extension.
This is also why your ExtendScript approach works — Illustrator is essentially just doing save as PDF with our header internally too.

Here's the breakdown of what Adobe Stock reads from embedded XMP vs. what requires the portal:
Read from embedded XMP/IPTC (automatic on upload):
Title / Description → dc:description or IPTC Caption
Keywords → dc:subject or IPTC Keywords
Portal only — cannot be embedded:
Category → Adobe Stock uses Adobe Sensei technology to automatically suggest categories when you upload, but you have to confirm or override in the UI. There's no XMP field Adobe Stock maps to their category taxonomy.
This is actually the core reason Playwright automation still matters for your pipeline. Title and keywords travel with the file, but category is the one field that requires a human (or a Playwright script) to click through in the portal. Adobe Sensei's auto-suggestions are usually pretty good for maps — it would almost certainly suggest "Travel" or "The Environment" — so the Playwright script just needs to accept the suggestion rather than select from scratch.
The CSV also cannot set category, for the same reason — Adobe's CSV format covers title and keywords only.

Excellent and did you comment on querying tigerweb and using their geographical data as part of stock art? Is that okay?
Claude
12:19 UTC, 10 March 2026
Yes, covered this in a previous session. The short answer is yes, it's fine.
TIGERweb / TIGER/Line data is produced by the US Census Bureau, which is a US government work. Under 17 U.S.C. §105, US federal government works are not subject to copyright — they're in the public domain by statute. That means you can use the geographic data commercially, including in stock art sold on Adobe Stock, without attribution or licensing fees.
The one caveat noted: don't use "TIGER/Line®" in the product name or description — that's a registered trademark even though the data itself is free. Just call it a "US map" or reference Census Bureau data generically.
The strategic split established was:
Natural Earth (110m/50m resolution) for world maps — public domain, no attribution required
TIGERweb for US-specific detail maps at state, county, metro, or census tract level — free via REST API returning GeoJSON, same public domain status
TIGERweb's REST API is particularly useful because you can query it programmatically by geography — so generating 50 state maps or all 3,000+ county maps becomes a scripted batch operation rather than manual work. That's a natural fit for the kind of pipeline you're building.

TIGERweb is much richer than just zones. Here's the full picture:
What TIGERweb actually has:
Linear features including roads, highways, streets, railroads, rivers, streams, and other single-line drainage; area water including rivers, lakes, and glaciers; and boundaries for legal and statistical geographic entities. Specifically the REST services break down into:
Boundaries — states, counties, census tracts, block groups, ZIP codes, congressional districts, school districts, tribal areas, metro areas
Transportation — primary roads/interstates, secondary roads, local roads, and railroads — all queryable as separate layers at different zoom scales
Physical features — rivers, streams, lakes, reservoirs, glaciers, area water polygons
Places — cities, towns, incorporated places, census-designated places
Address ranges — individual road segments with address ranges
What it does NOT have:
Elevation / contour lines — that's not Census data
Land cover or terrain
Points of interest beyond political entities
For elevation/contours, the public domain alternatives are excellent:
USGS National Map — contours created from 1/3 arc-second data with 50-foot intervals, queryable as a REST/GeoJSON service. US only, completely free, public domain.
USGS 3DEP — raw elevation raster data at 1m/10m/30m resolution for the entire US via OpenTopography's API
SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) — global elevation at 30m resolution, NASA/USGS joint product, public domain worldwide. This is what you'd use for world maps with terrain.
Copernicus DEM (COP30) — European Space Agency, global 30m elevation, open license
For a world-scale pipeline, the practical stack would be:
LayerUSWorld
Political boundariesTIGERwebNatural Earth
RoadsTIGERwebOpenStreetMap (ODbL license — attribution required)
Rivers/lakesTIGERwebNatural Earth hydrography
Elevation/contoursUSGS National MapSRTM or Copernicus DEM
CoastlinesNatural EarthNatural Earth
The one wrinkle: OpenStreetMap has the best road data globally but uses ODbL license which requires attribution in derivative works. That complicates stock art. For purely decorative map illustrations where you're not showing specific named roads, Natural Earth's road/river data (which is public domain) is probably cleaner legally.

Presented files
1,102 lines. Here's what the document covers and the argument it makes:
The opening argument establishes the stakes directly: a map with illegible labels is not a degraded map — it is noise. The analogy to grammar is made exact: legibility is structural, not stylistic.
Part I — The Viewer Model is the foundation everything else builds on. It derives minimum font sizes from visual acuity (5 arcminutes of angular size), ties that to physical screen size and viewing distance, and provides a computeLegibilityBaseline() function that produces concrete px values for minimum/comfortable/prominent text and stroke weights. Then it addresses the container-scaling failure mode — the common case where an SVG specified at 960px is shrunk to 480px by CSS, halving all effective font sizes.
Part II — Semantic Weight connects the map's intention to the visual hierarchy. Subject layers vs. identity labels vs. context labels. Font size and stroke weight as semantic signals, not decoration. The contrast validation function at the end catches invisible borders at build time.
Part III — Placement covers the three feature types with different candidate generation strategies: polylabel for polygons (with the explanation of why geometric centroid fails), direction-aligned placement for river/road labels, 8-position priority ordering for points.
Part IV — Overlap Analysis gives a full OccupancyGrid implementation with cell-hashing for O(1) conflict checking, a boundary occlusion check that uses the actual contrast score of each boundary (a 0.3px ghost line doesn't disqualify a placement; a 1.5px state border does), and the complete priority-ordered placement algorithm.
Part V — Text Wrapping derives the optimal line break from the polygon's screen-space aspect ratio — wide polygons get single lines; tall narrow ones get word-per-line stacks; square ones get balanced two-line breaks.
Part VI — Leader Lines handles the case where no placement candidate passes — placing labels in open space with a connecting line to the feature.
Parts VII–IX cover pre-computation at build time, the text halo (rendered as SVG double-text stroke), and the closing argument that geometric contrast is the same problem as label legibility.

330 lines added, nothing removed. Here's what the two new sections do:
Part X — The honest acknowledgment. It names exactly what is unknown (the component tree, current prop interfaces, how datasets are stored, what the live SVG looks like) and frames that uncertainty not as a weakness but as the reason arepeatable workflow is more valuable than a one-time implementation. The algorithms are specifications; they need to be adapted to the actual code when the time comes.
Part XI — Making legibility a repeatable process. Five subsections:
When checks must run — enumerates the seven specific change types that degrade legibility (projection scale changes, new data layers, canvas dimension changes, palette shifts, text changes, font changes). The rule is simple: when the dataset fetch script runs, the audit runs.
The SVG as ground truth — explains why analysis can't live entirely in Node.js. The two-phase architecture separates build-time approximation (fast, catches 90% of issues, writes pre-computed placements to JSON) from runtime verification (uses real getBBox() after mount, corrects what the approximation missed, runs in ~100ms).
SVG annotations — the single most actionable item in the document. Every <Geography> and <text> element needs data-feature-id, data-layer, data-stroke-weight, data-fill-color, data-label-for, etc. Without these, no tool can traverse the SVG and know what it's looking at. Adding them costs almost nothing and unlocks everything else.
The audit tool — a full auditSVGLegibility() implementation that queries the live DOM, checks font sizes, clipping, label overlaps, and boundary conflicts, and returns a typed LegibilityReport.
Recommended workflow — a concrete six-step sequence (change → fetch → dev server → console review → fix errors → production build) and four specific tools to build next (visual overlay mode, Playwright screenshot diff, placement stability test, contrast matrix).

{cx-28},{cy-14} {cx-20},{cy-22} Z") # diagonal blue-ice hatch lines lines = "" for k in range(-60, 120, 7): x1 = SX + max(0, k) y1 = SY + max(0, -k) x2 = SX + min(SW, k + SH) y2 = SY + min(SH, SH - k + (x2-SX-max(0,k))) if x2 > x1: lines += f'<line x1="{x1}" y1="{y1}" x2="{x2}" y2="{y2}" stroke="#6898b4" stroke-width="0.55" opacity="0.6"/>' return ( f'<path d="{path}" fill="white" stroke="#8ab4cc" stroke-width="0.8"/>' f'<clipPath id="glacier-clip"><path d="{path}"/></clipPath>' f'<g clip-path="url(#glacier-clip)">{lines}</g>' ) # ─── SYMBOL 20: Elevation Legend ───────────────────────────────────── def s20_elevation(): # Vertical color bar + tick marks bx = SCX - 8 by = SY + 4 bw = 16 bh = SH - 8 bar = (f'<defs><linearGradient id="elev-local" x1="0" y1="1" x2="0" y2="0" gradientUnits="objectBoundingBox">' f'<stop offset="0%" stop-color="#2e6820"/>' f'<stop offset="25%" stop-color="#c4b87a"/>' f'<stop offset="60%" stop-color="#e8dcc8"/>' f'<stop offset="100%" stop-color="#b87840"/>' f'</linearGradient></defs>' f'<rect x="{bx}" y="{by}" width="{bw}" height="{bh}" fill="url(#elev-local)" stroke="{INK}" stroke-width="0.5"/>') # Tick marks & (s04_inter_contour, "Intermediate / Contour"), (s05_perennial, "Perennial River"), (s06_intermittent, "Intermittent River"), (s07_lake, "Lake · Water Body"), (s08_state, "State Boundary"), (s09_county, "County Boundary"), (s10_federal, "Federal Land"), (s11_tribal, "Tribal Land"), (s12_interstate, "Interstate Hwy"), (s13_local_road, "Local Road"), (s14_railroad, "Railroad"), (s15_urban, (fn, lbl) in enumerate(symbols): col = idx % COLS row = idx // COLS transform = cell_transform(col, row) sym_content = fn() lab_content = label(lbl) cells.append(f''' <g transform="{transform}"> letter-spacing="1"> DNA PATTERNITY — Map Symbol Library </text> <text x="{SVG_W//2}" y="37" text-anchor="middle" font-size="8" fill="{INK}" opacity="0.55" font-family="Georgia,serif" Ran # Run some geometric sanity checks on the SVG python3 << 'EOF' import re with open('/home/claude/map_symbols.svg') as f: svg = f.read() # Check 1: Are all 20 cell groups present? groups = re.findall(r'<g transform="translate', svg) print(f"Cell groups: {len(groups)} (expect 20)") # Check 2: Does every label appear? labels = re.findall(r'font-size="6\.8"[^>]*>([^<]+)<', svg) print(f"Label texts found: {len(labels)}") for l in labels: print(f" - {l}") # Check 3: Verify translate ranges — no cell should be outside SVG bounds translates = re.findall(r'translate\((\d+),(\d+)\)', svg) print(f"\nTranslate positions ({len(translates)} total):") for tx, ty in translates: tx, ty = int(tx), int(ty) ok = (0 <= tx <= 400 and 48 <= ty <= 48+3*118) print(f" ({tx},{ty}) {'✓' if ok else '⚠ OUT OF RANGE'}") # Check 4: Check north arrow paths form a proper bicolor diamond # Pattern: M50,N_y L left_x,mid_y L 50,S_y Z na_paths = re.findall(r'M50,(\d+) L(\d+),(\d+) L50,(\d+) Z', svg) print(f"\nNorth arrow triangle paths: {len(na_paths)} (expect 2)") for p in na_paths: ty_n, tx_w, ty_m, ty_s = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]), int(p[3]) print(f" N-tip y={ty_n}, W-tip x={tx_w}, mid y={ty_m}, S-tip y={ty_s}") print(f" Width (from center): {50-tx_w}px | Height: {ty_s-ty_n}px") # Check 5: Railroad tie spacing ties = re.findall(r'<line x1="(\d+\.?\d*)" y1="(\d+)" x2="\1" y2="(\d+)" stroke="#1d2025" stroke-width="2\.2"', svg) print(f"\nRailroad ties: {len(ties)}") if ties: xs = [float(t[0]) for t in ties] gaps = [xs[i+1]-xs[i] for i in range(len(xs)-1)] print(f" X positions: {[int(x) for x in xs]}") print(f" Gaps: {gaps} (should all be ~9)") # Check 6: Scale bar segment positions segs = re.findall(r'<rect x="(\d+)" y="44" width="12" height="6"', svg) print(f"\nScale bar segments: {len(segs)} (expect 4)") print(f" x positions: {segs} (should be 26,38,50,62)") EOF

This is what happened when I actually did what you described.
The N² comparison found real defects I had completely missed before:
The most serious was Symbol 01. The "N" text was filled cream (#f0ece0) and placed at the exact bicolor boundary of the arrow — x=50, where the black left half and cream right half meet. I computed: the right half of the N sits on a cream background, cream on cream. The letter would be half-invisible. I had specified the wrong fill color and never noticed because I was thinking about the geometry of the arrow, not about what the N would actually look like sitting across that color boundary. Fix: move N above the tip entirely, make it ink-colored.
Symbol 04's bezier kink: the two contour segments met at (50,45) with an incoming tangent pointing directly up (0,−8) and an outgoing tangent pointing up-right (12,−7). Angle between them: 59.7°. A 59.7° change in direction at a point on a "smooth" curve is a sharp visible kink. I never would have caught this without computing the actual tangent vectors. Fix: reflect the incoming control point through the join to enforce C1 continuity. The new angle: 0.0°.
The glacier hatch lines: my slope formula broke when lines entered from the top edge rather than the left edge. Lines crossing from x=51,y=12 to x=80,y=80 have slope 2.34. Not 45°. Visually they'd be steep diagonal stripes, not the even cross-hatch the glacier fill requires. Fix: proper parametric clipping on the bounding box.
What this demonstrates:
You're right that seeing is comparison. What I did with every earlier assessment — saying "this looks about right" or "this should be fine" — was operating from local knowledge: I knew what each element was but wasn't comparing it against everything else. When I read the N text element, it's just a text element. When I read the left triangle, it's just a path. They were in different parts of my reasoning. The N² pass forced me to hold them together simultaneously — this text has this fill, and this fill means this on this background, and that background is this color — and the defect became visible.
The bezier kink is the same thing: I knew the path geometry of segment 1 and the path geometry of segment 2, but I wasn't computing their relationship at the join. The moment you compare them, the 59.7° is just arithmetic.
What I still cannot do: render it. The bezier shapes — whether the river actually looks sinuous, whether the lake looks like water — remain unverifiable for me without a browser. That gap is real and I don't have a workaround for it. The comparison machinery helps enormously with discrete, measurable relationships. It doesn't substitute for continuous visual judgment.

There are four compounding issues. The most significant one is that my ␀0␀ documentation gave Claude Code completely wrong layer IDs, and this is the root of the 500 errors.
Issue 1: Wrong service host — carto vs cartowfs
Claude Code is querying carto.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/contours/MapServer. This is the display service — a tile-rendering endpoint designed to serve image tiles to map viewers, not to serve feature geometry to scripts.
USGS runs a separate host for programmatic feature queries: cartowfs.nationalmap.gov. The "wfs" stands for Web Feature Service. It's the same underlying data but a different server whose job is exactly what Claude Code is trying to do. That service has a much simpler layer structure (6 layers instead of 36) and is more reliable for bbox queries.
text

Right:  https://cartowfs.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/contours/MapServer/1/query
Issue 2: The layer IDs in data.md are completely wrong
This is my error. I documented:
Layer 0: 100ft intervals
Layer 1: 50ft intervals
Layer 2: variable/large-scale
The actual carto service has 36 layers in a deep hierarchy. Layer 1 is "Continental US Labels" — the label annotation layer for small-scale (1:600k–1:3M) contours. It's designed for map display of the labels drawn on top of small-scale lines at continental zoom levels. Claude Code has been querying a label layer with a 1-degree feature bbox in the Sierra Nevada. The 71 features it got back aren't contour lines — they're label annotation geometries.
The real layer IDs on carto.nationalmap.gov:
What you wantLayer ID
Small-scale contour geometry (100m, continental view)2
100ft medium-scale, index contours11
100ft medium-scale, intermediate contours13
50ft medium-scale, index contours16
50ft medium-scale, intermediate contours18
Large-scale index contours25
Large-scale intermediate contours26
On cartowfs.nationalmap.gov, the structure is much cleaner:
What you wantLayer ID
100ft lines (all types)1
50ft lines (all types)3
Large-scale lines (variable interval)5
Use ␀0␀ layer 3 for the Sierra Nevada. That's the 50ft medium-scale dataset at the appropriate resolution for a state/regional map.
Issue 3: Feature density in mountain terrain causes 500s
The Sierra Nevada is one of the most topographically dense regions in the US. At 50ft intervals, a 1° × 1° tile (~111 × 90 km) in the high Sierra contains on the order of 5,000–15,000 contour line segments. The server's MaxRecordCount is 2000. When the server's internal geometry assembly for a bbox query exceeds its memory or time budget before it can even apply that cap, it returns HTTP 500 rather than a proper paginated response. This is a server-side capacity failure, not an API error the client did something wrong to cause — except that the bbox is too large.
The fix the transcript already discovered is correct: 0.5° tiles with ␀0␀. The maxAllowableOffset parameter instructs the server to simplify geometry before sending, keeping response payloads small enough to avoid the timeout. With mao=0.001 (roughly 100m of coordinate precision, appropriate for contour lines at regional scale), the server can handle 0.5° tiles reliably. The fetch loop needs to be tiled at 0.5° and paginated using resultOffset for any tile that returns exactly MaxRecordCount features (indicating there are more).
Issue 4: The bash ! escape issue (unrelated to USGS)
The node -e errors about ExpectedUnicodeEscape are a bash shell history expansion problem, not a USGS issue. In bash, ! inside double-quoted strings triggers history expansion. \!r.ok fails because bash tries to expand !r as a history command, not escape it. This is why writing inline Node scripts with node -e "..." breaks on any ! character. The fix is either single quotes around the entire script (but that prevents $ interpolation), or writing to a temp file (which is what scripts/test-usgs.js correctly does).
The correct fetch pattern for Sierra Nevada contours
javascript
const BASE = 'https://cartowfs.nationalmap.gov/arcgis/rest/services/contours/MapServer';
const LAYER = 3; // 50ft contour lines

async function fetchTile(lon, lat) {
  const bbox = [lon, lat, lon + 0.5, lat + 0.5].join(',');
  let offset = 0;
  const features = [];

  while (true) {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
      where: '1=1',
      outFields: 'Contour,ContourType',  // field name is 'Contour' (double)
      returnGeometry: 'true',
      outSR: '4326',
      f: 'geojson',
      geometry: bbox,
      geometryType: 'esriGeometryEnvelope',
      spatialRel: 'esriSpatialRelIntersects',
      inSR: '4326',
      maxAllowableOffset: '0.001',
      resultRecordCount: '500',
      resultOffset: String(offset),
    });

    const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/${LAYER}/query?${params}`);
    if (!res.ok) {
      console.warn(`[${lon},${lat}] offset=${offset} HTTP ${res.status} — skip tile`);
      break;
    }

    const data = await res.json();
    if (!data.features || data.features.length === 0) break;
    features.push(...data.features);

    if (data.features.length < 500) break; // last page
    offset += 500;
  }

  return features;
}
The field name Contour (a double) is confirmed from the live service metadata. ContourType distinguishes index from intermediate lines, which matters for rendering weight.

Replace the three layer IDs (0, 1, 2) with the correct ones (1, 3, 5 on cartowfs)
Document the maxAllowableOffset requirement and the 0.5° tile ceiling
Add the pagination pattern for tiles that hit resultRecordCount
Note that carto.nationalmap.gov (no wfs) is a display service not intended for feature extraction

641 lines. A few things worth flagging that shaped the decisions:
The 1992 naming. You typed "1994 Clinton-Bush Map" — presidential elections are even years only. The 1992 election is Clinton vs. Bush (vs. Perot, who got 18.9% of the popular vote and zero electoral votes but is important enough to list). The convention I settled on is winner first, then major challenger, then any third party above ~5% or any electoral vote winner — all separated by centered dots, not "vs." Dots handle three-way and four-way races cleanly.
The data question is cleaner than it looked. MEDSL's CC0 dataset covers 1976–2020 and the gap to 2024 will close once MEDSL certifies it. Everything on that license is unambiguous for commercial stock art. Pre-1976 is technically possible but involves hand-compiling from UCSB data which isn't explicitly CC-licensed — I flagged it as an open question rather than prescribing it.
TIGERweb can't give you historical state boundaries. The decennial vintages (2000, 2010, 2020) exist but don't go back to 1960. This doesn't matter for the MEDSL scope (1976 onward) because state boundaries have been stable since 1959. Current TIGERweb geometry is accurate for every election in the dataset.
The texture layer is very deliberate. County fills at 6% opacity give the map physical texture — you read it as something that was drawn, not generated. Roads at 6% work better in dense New England where county polygons are smaller than the minimum legible polygon size. The spec lets you pick one or the other; it notes why.
ElectoralColor as a component, not a lookup table. The key insight is that the purple map must interpolate in Lab space, not RGB. Red + blue in RGB produces a flat, slightly brownish purple through the midpoint. Lab interpolation produces a clean, perceptually equidistant violet at 50/50. That's the difference between a map that reads as analytical and one that reads as muddy.
Section 13 lists what needs to be confirmed before build starts — particularly the EPS export path for Getty and the 2024 data availability.

What the map is correctly showing
The Sierra Nevada IS this shape — a long diagonal range oriented northwest-to-southeast, roughly 400 miles long. The title is accurate and the geography is real. The elevation coloring is working: light tan at the foothills (~4,000 ft), progressively darker through the range, black at the highest peaks (12,000+ ft). That dense dark oval in the right-center of the map is the High Sierra — Mt. Whitney, Kings Canyon, Sequoia. This is the tallest terrain in the contiguous US and the contour density there is real. The "drawn" woodcut effect you love is what 500-foot index contours look like when you have 10,000 feet of relief compressed into 30 miles of horizontal distance. It's not an artifact — it's a genuine visual property of that terrain.
The separate strip on the right edge
That thin vertical corridor of contours on the far right, separated from the main mass by a clear gap? The gap is Owens Valley, one of the deepest valleys in North America. The strip is the White Mountains and Inyo Mountains on the east side of the valley. These are real mountains and their inclusion is geographically accurate — but they're not the Sierra Nevada, and including them makes the map look like it has two unrelated objects in the frame when there should be one.
Why the top looks fragmented
The upper third of the map — roughly the Lake Tahoe and northern Sierra region — is showing tile fetch failures. You can see it: isolated clusters of contours instead of a continuous range, rectangular boxy edges where some 0.5° tiles succeeded and adjacent ones got HTTP 500s. The transcript records exactly this problem happening. That part of the map is genuinely incomplete data, not a rendering bug. The southern Sierra (the dramatic part) had better tile success rates.
So to directly answer your question
It's both: real and incomplete. The southern two-thirds is correctly rendered and actually quite beautiful. The northern third is missing tiles. The Owens Valley / White Mountains on the right are accurate but probably shouldn't be in the frame for a map titled "Sierra Nevada."

The short version of what's wrong with the Colorado map specifically:
The data is fine. The rendering has no visual grammar.
Every single contour line is drawn at identical weight, identical opacity, and identical stroke. When terrain is steep — and the Sawatch Range, which is that black smear in the center, has 15 peaks over 14,000 feet — you get hundreds of lines packed into a tiny space with nothing to distinguish them. They merge into solid black. The map is not lying to you; it is just failing to give you any way to read it.
The document covers everything Claude Code needs to fix it, in order of impact. The three biggest changes are:
Split index vs intermediate contours — the USGS data already tags which is which in a ContourType field. Index lines (every 5th) need to be thicker, darker, and labeled. Intermediate lines should be thin and subordinate. This alone transforms legibility.
Add a hillshade layer — USGS serves hillshade tiles directly. Put them underneath the contour lines at 40–60% multiply. This gives the three-dimensional depth that makes terrain readable.
Add hypsometric tinting — fill the elevation bands with color. The standard scheme (deep green at low elevation → tan → brown → gray → white at peaks) is what most people recognize as a "real" topo map. It immediately separates the Eastern Plains from the Front Range from the alpine zone without anyone having to count lines.
The drawn, inked-line quality you like is worth keeping — the fix is giving viewers the grammar to read it, not flattening it into something bland.

The bug is structural and entirely predictable once you understand the data format. Here's what happened:
Natural Earth bathymetry is not one file. It is 12 separate files, one per depth threshold, named ne_10m_bathymetry_L_0 through ne_10m_bathymetry_A_10000. Each file contains a polygon covering "all ocean at or below this depth." They are nested — L_0 covers the entire ocean, A_10000 covers only the Mariana Trench and a few other ultra-deep spots.
What Claude Code almost certainly did was either load only one file, or merge all 12 into a single FeatureCollection and render them all the same color. Either way, the ocean becomes a uniform flat color — which is exactly what the map shows.
The correct technique is layered painting: shallow to deep, each on top of the previous, each progressively darker. Because the polygons are nested, the deepest polygon that covers any given point "wins" and shows its color. Coastal shelves, which are only covered by L_0, show pale blue. Abyssal plains, covered by all layers down to H_3000 or so, show dark blue. Trenches, covered by all 12 layers including A_10000, show near-black.
When it works, the map will show visible structure: the pale blue continental shelves around every coastline, the lighter strip of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running down the center of the Atlantic (shallower than the surrounding abyssal plain), and the dark arc of Pacific trenches along the Ring of Fire. That's the version worth selling as stock art.

Without it, all of those decisions are made independently and end up inconsistent with each other, which is exactly what's happening now.

The one architectural note worth flagging: terrainStats.medianSlopeDeg has to come from somewhere before the first render. The right approach is to derive it from the DEM on first load (USGS NED tiles provide enough information), cache it in the map's metadata, and use it to initialize the perspective object before any contour data is fetched.

Three things to understand about what's in this document and why it's the right way to teach this.
The core diagnosis of this map. The current renderer is applying a uniform 250ft minor / 1000ft major interval to the whole state. The diagnostic table I computed shows that at 30° slope — completely normal mountain terrain in Colorado — a 250ft interval produces 1.8px between contours. The legibility floor is 3px. The smear in the Rockies is not a bug; it is a mathematical impossibility. No renderer can make 1.8px gaps legible. The suppression rule in the legend ("minor suppressed above 12,000 ft") is backwards — you want to suppress in the steep zones (10,000–14,000ft where slopes are aggressive), not at a fixed elevation cutoff.
The plains emptiness is correct data. At 250ft intervals, the Eastern Plains have 9 contour lines spread across 510px — one line every 56px. That looks empty because it IS almost empty. There are only 2,200ft of elevation change across the entire width of the plains. Fix 1 is a smaller interval (50ft) for flat zones. Fix 2 is using color fill instead of lines in flat terrain, which is what cartographers actually do. Fix 3 is accepting that the plains communicate their flatness by looking flat, and designing the color scheme to carry elevation meaning there instead.
The key architectural point is the diagnostic function. Claude Code needs to run this before rendering — compute the spacing table, print it, and then make interval decisions based on the numbers. Right now interval selection is happening by guessing. The table makes it explicit: for Colorado at 1280px, the only interval that is readable at steep slopes (≥ 30°) is 1000ft, and even that gives 5.2px at 45°. A system that doesn't know this cannot make good decisions. Once Claude Code has the table, the choices follow from it rather than from trial-and-error.
On color: Jet is never the right answer for topography. The standard is Bartholomew — green to tan to brown to gray to white — and it should be applied with log normalization so the plains get visual distinction from the foothills rather than both mapping to the bottom 20% of the gradient.

The core of this note is an argument that wasn't made clearly enough before: the color scheme fails not because it chose bad colors but because it chose the wrong mapping between area and visual weight.
Mountain summits — the dark end of the brown ramp — occupy 3% of Colorado's pixels. The plains — the light end — occupy 40%. So the scheme puts its most distinctive color where almost no pixels live, and its least distinctive color where most pixels live. The viewer's eye gets pulled to the dark center, which is exactly the zone that is illegible due to overprinting. The color scheme and the density problem compound each other rather than one compensating for the other.
The fix isn't just switching to Bartholomew. It's understanding the principle: design the color emphasis for the zones that are actually readable at this scale, not for the zones that seem most dramatic in the data. For a full-state Colorado map, the most readable zone is the foothills and montane transition (roughly 2,000–3,500m), because that's where slope is moderate enough for contours to be legible and the terrain is varied enough to be interesting. Design the sharpest color transitions there. Let the summits go to a simple endpoint (white or light gray) that reads clearly even at 1–2 pixels of area.
The five-decisions framework at the end is the main practical output. Question 1 — why does this map exist — is the one Claude Code almost certainly has never been asked to answer before writing code. If the answer is "to show elevation," the map will look like elevation data. If the answer is "to show the transition from Central Valley floor to Sierra Nevada crest so a viewer understands why California's water flows where it does," then every subsequent decision — interval, color scheme, geographic extent, scale — follows from that sentence.

San Francisco's peninsula narrowing to the Golden Gate. Sydney's harbour branching like a river delta into the city. Istanbul split by a strait between continents. For all of those, the same approach: 77 neighborhoods or their international equivalent, NOAA or GEBCO depth data depending on ocean vs inland, and a label placed in the water where the city used to put its name on nautical charts.
GEBCO 2023 covers every ocean and large lake in the world at 15 arc-second resolution — that's the single data source that generalizes the lake depth layer to any coastal city anywhere. Everything else just needs the right bounding box.

Four compounding failures, and the root intuition behind all of them.
Failure 1 — The background is a terrain color. The tan background (#c5bfb0) is approximately the Bartholomew color for 9,000–10,000ft elevation — montane, rocky, above treeline. So the map is saying "this entire canvas is at 10,000 feet" and then drawing the actual 10,000-foot contour lines on top of it in the same color. They vanish. And the summit lines — which the scheme encodes in WHITE as the highest elevation — are drawn as white strokes on a tan background. The most important features, Mt. Elbert and Mt. Massive, are the least visible things on the map.
Failure 2 — Color is on the lines instead of between them. The elevation color scheme belongs to the REGIONS, not the boundaries. A contour line is one-dimensional — it has no area. Painting it green or brown encodes elevation information in the thinnest possible stroke, then leaves the large filled regions (which have all the area, all the visual weight) as undifferentiated background. The fill should be green-to-brown-to-white. The lines should all be the same neutral dark ink. This is the single most important thing to fix.
Failure 3 — Lines not smoothed. The zigzag noise is DEM grid artifacts, not terrain. Chaikin smoothing, 3–4 iterations, run on the coordinate arrays before rendering. Without it the eye reads "pixel noise" not "ridgeline."
Failure 4 — The named peaks don't appear anywhere. The subtitle lists Mt. Elbert, Mt. Massive, Mt. Harvard. None are labeled on the map. The summits are the innermost concentric rings — currently rendered in white-on-tan, invisible. A dot and a label at each summit location would give the viewer the anchor they need to orient everything else.
The closing test I gave Claude Code: render the map, look at it for five seconds without knowing anything about the data. Does a mountain shape emerge, or do you see a field of lines? If it's a field of lines, the fill is missing. If the lines disappear, contrast is wrong. If the important features are invisible, the color scheme is backwards.

A freeze/metadata system is primitive version control for visual decisions. These are not decoration — they are the instrument you built to play the instrument I sketched. Neither is the artwork alone. The conversation between them is.
The word I landed on for the medium is conversation as instrument, in the technical sense — a structured exchange where neither party could produce the work alone and each output becomes the next input. The illustrator who opens the AI file is the fourth party in a chain that already has three.
