The author of this project — Doug — asked a specific question before making this assignment: did I see the signature, and did I understand the margins? Both answers follow, because they change how you must think about the work you are about to do.* --- ### On the Signature At the bottom center of the Chicago frame, barely readable: *Source: DNA Atlas ♥ https://atlas.love ♥ Doug & Ana* DNA. Doug and Ana. The name of the project encodes the names of its makers. The signature is not metadata — it is not a tooltip or a data attribution. It is a maker's mark, the kind a printmaker presses into the lower corner of an edition. Its smallness is precisely calibrated: it is present enough to be found by someone looking, invisible enough not to interrupt the reading of someone looking at the work. Every one of the ten new pieces you are about to make should carry this same mark, in the same position, at the same size. It is part of the visual grammar of the series. --- ### On the Margins Look carefully at where the road lines meet the frame edge in the Chicago piece. Some lines — the expressways — exit the frame completely. They do not stop short of the edge. They run all the way to it and continue beyond, as if the frame is a window onto something larger. Other lines — the roads that terminate at the lake — stop in the middle of the picture, wherever the water begins. There is no padding, no forced breathing room, no artificial margin between road network and frame. This is not a technical oversight. It is the composition's argument: the city is too large for the frame and the frame knows it. The expressways were already going somewhere before this picture started and they will keep going after it ends. The lake is the only thing that actually stops them. **Do not pad the bounding box to create artificial margins.** The margins in this work emerge from the data. The frame edge cuts the urban fabric wherever the bbox coordinates fall. Some roads will exit the frame. That is correct. The bbox is a viewing window, not a container. One exception: if a bounding box edge falls in empty rural territory, with no roads near the frame edge, that side will have a natural soft margin. This is also correct. Let it be. --- ### What the Series Is About The Chicago piece is not a map of Chicago. It is an argument about a specific type of city: a city that does not taper at the edges, does not dissolve gradually into countryside, but instead terminates — sharply, absolutely — against water. The lake does not surround Chicago. The lake *defines* it. The city fills all available land and goes no further. The ten cities in this series are chosen because each of them has a water relationship so central to its identity that removing the water from the picture would make the city unreadable. In each case the void created by water — the unmarked, road-free negative space — is as compositionally necessary as the marks themselves. The title, in every case, will float in that void. This is not a label. It is an acknowledgment that the city's name belongs to the place the city cannot be. Each piece will differ in *where* the water falls: left, right, top, bottom, center, or multiple edges. These variations produce different emotional registers. Water on the left or right creates a clean directional reading — horizon. Water at the bottom creates a sense of the city pouring toward something. Water in the center (between two urban zones) creates tension. Water at multiple edges creates enclosure, island-ness. Choose the bounding box for each city with this register in mind, not just with coverage accuracy. --- ### The Selector Control Add a city selector dropdown as the **topmost control**, above all others including Map Title. It must say: ``` CHICAGO ``` when the Chicago map is active. The dropdown should contain eleven items total: CHICAGO plus the ten cities below. When a new city is selected, the following must all change simultaneously: - The road data displayed (fetched and cached per city on first load; do not re-fetch on switching) - The SVG viewport / aspect ratio / canvas dimensions - The title text (to match the city name, as a starting default) - The title position (x, y coordinates in SVG space matching the water void for that city) - The frame (the frame must reflow to fit the new aspect ratio while maintaining even border width) All other controls — MAP TITLE, MAP FRAME, MAP BACKGROUND — remain visible and function identically for all cities. When a user customizes a title position for one city, that customization is local to that city and does not affect others. **Folder structure.** The existing Chicago implementation lives in a folder. Create ten new sibling folders, one per city, named exactly: ``` manhattan san-francisco seattle miami hong-kong istanbul sydney mumbai rio-de-janeiro lisbon ``` Each folder contains its city's OSM data cache file (JSON). The selector control is the mechanism by which the user moves between them. --- ### The Overpass Query Template All cities use the same Overpass query structure. The endpoint is `https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter`. The query, parameterized by bounding box `[S,W,N,E]`: ``` [out:json][timeout:60]; ( way["highway"~"motorway|motorway_link|trunk|trunk_link"](S,W,N,E); way["highway"~"primary|primary_link"](S,W,N,E); way["highway"~"secondary|tertiary"](S,W,N,E); way["highway"~"residential|unclassified|living_street"](S,W,N,E); ); out geom qt; ``` The `qt` modifier sorts results spatially, which speeds rendering. After fetching, group ways by their `highway` tag into four tiers for styling. The tiers and their visual properties are: | Tier | Tags | Stroke Weight | Stroke Color | Opacity | |------|------|--------------|--------------|---------| | 1 — Arterial | motorway, motorway_link, trunk, trunk_link | 2.0–2.5px | `#1a1a1a` | 1.0 | | 2 — Primary | primary, primary_link | 1.2–1.5px | `#1a1a1a` | 0.85 | | 3 — Secondary | secondary, tertiary | 0.7px | `#333333` | 0.6 | | 4 — Local | residential, unclassified, living_street | 0.35px | `#555555` | 0.25 | Render in reverse tier order: Tier 4 first (bottom), Tier 1 last (top). This is the same technique used in the Chicago map to produce the pencil/pen quality — the ghost of the local grid visible beneath the assertion of the arterials. Look at the existing Chicago implementation carefully before building these. The specific stroke weights and opacities that produce the pencil quality are calibrated in that code. Match them. Do not approximate. --- ### The Ten Cities For each city: the bounding box is given as `[S, W, N, E]` in decimal degrees (negative = south or west). The canvas dimensions are width × height in SVG units. The water position describes where the void falls. The title position is approximate SVG coordinates (percentage of canvas width/height) for where to float the city name in the water. --- #### 1. NEW YORK — Manhattan Island **Water relationship:** The Hudson River erases the left side of the frame; the East River erases the right. Manhattan is a corridor of marks between two voids. **Bounding box:** `[40.698, -74.025, 40.820, -73.907]` **Canvas dimensions:** 1100 × 700 (landscape — the island runs left to right at this proportion) **What you will see:** The island appears as a dense central band of marks, wider and more gridded in midtown, more organic at the edges. The Hudson void dominates the bottom-left; the East River void is narrower on the right. The grid of streets is among the most regular on Earth — the Commissioners' Plan of 1811 — interrupted by Broadway's diagonal slash and by the organic paths of the pre-grid lower island. The West Side Highway/FDR Drive will read as clean arterial lines tracing the water's edge. **Title:** "NEW YORK" — place in the Hudson River void, lower-left quadrant of the canvas, roughly at x=8%, y=75% of canvas dimensions. **Note:** The NJ waterfront may show faintly as light ghost lines across the Hudson. This is correct and beautiful — it makes the water legible as water rather than as simply an empty rectangle. --- #### 2. SAN FRANCISCO **Water relationship:** The Pacific Ocean erases the left edge; the San Francisco Bay erases the right. The peninsula tapers toward the north (toward the Golden Gate) — the city becomes an arrowhead pointing at the gap between two waters. **Bounding box:** `[37.705, -122.520, 37.830, -122.353]` **Canvas dimensions:** 900 × 1000 (portrait — the peninsula is taller than wide at this crop) **What you will see:** The street grid in the center of the city is hyperregular — the classic SF grid imposed regardless of terrain, producing blocks that climb improbable hills. The Sunset District in the west will read as an exceptionally uniform grid. The bay shore on the right will have the highway infrastructure visible. Twin Peaks and other hilltop parks will appear as voids within the urban fabric — no roads. **Title:** "SAN FRANCISCO" — in the bay, right side, at approximately x=78%, y=45%. The bay shore provides a natural left edge for the text. --- #### 3. SEATTLE **Water relationship:** Elliott Bay and Puget Sound erase the left (west) side of the frame. This is the most Chicago-like composition in the series — city crowds the right, water is the left void. The arrangement is nearly a mirror of Chicago. **Bounding box:** `[47.555, -122.430, 47.730, -122.210]` **Canvas dimensions:** 1200 × 650 (landscape) **What you will see:** The downtown core in the upper-left portion of the urban mass will show as dense arterial convergence. Interstates 5 and 90 will read as heavy structural lines. Lake Washington (eastern edge of the urban area, partly within bbox) will create a secondary void on the right — Seattle is actually bounded by water on both sides, Puget Sound to the west and the lake to the east, though the lake is less dramatic than the Sound. **Title:** "SEATTLE" — in Elliott Bay, upper-left, at approximately x=10%, y=25%. **Note:** If Lake Washington appears on the right edge, this is correct. Unlike Chicago's absolutely clean eastern edge, Seattle's double water relationship gives the piece a slightly different charge — the city is squeezed rather than simply bordered. --- #### 4. MIAMI — The Island Between Two Waters **Water relationship:** Biscayne Bay on the left (west), the Atlantic Ocean on the right (east). Miami Beach is an island between them. The MacArthur, Julia Tuttle, and other causeways cross the bay — thin lines over water. **Bounding box:** `[25.730, -80.220, 25.875, -80.100]` **Canvas dimensions:** 800 × 1100 (portrait — Miami Beach is an elongated island, taller than wide) **What you will see:** The city of Miami proper appears on the far left, across the bay. Miami Beach occupies the center as a long narrow island. The bay is a wide void in the left third of the frame. The ocean is a void on the right. The causeways are thin lines bridging the bay void — they are unlike anything in the Chicago piece. They make the water visible not just as absence of marks but as *something that had to be crossed*. **Title:** "MIAMI" — in the Atlantic Ocean, right side, at approximately x=88%, y=35%. **Important note:** Miami is a subtropical city. OSM data for Miami Beach may include residential streets in the Art Deco district that are extremely dense and on a very fine grid — the local tier lines may produce a beautiful tight texture there. Do not suppress them. At 800×1100 the residential grid of Miami Beach should be legible. --- #### 5. HONG KONG — The Harbour as Dividing Line **Water relationship:** Victoria Harbour is a horizontal void in the middle of the composition, separating Kowloon (the urban mass at the top) from Hong Kong Island (the urban mass at the bottom). Water is not at the edge — it is the center. This is the most radically different composition in the series. **Bounding box:** `[22.255, 114.095, 114.240, 22.388]` Wait — note on coordinate order. Overpass wants `[S, W, N, E]`: `[22.255, 114.095, 22.388, 114.240]` **Canvas dimensions:** 1200 × 700 (landscape) **What you will see:** Kowloon fills the upper third of the frame with extraordinary road density — one of the most road-dense areas on Earth. Victoria Harbour occupies the middle horizontal band as a void. Hong Kong Island's north face shows dense arterials along the harbour front (Connaught Road, Queen's Road). The MTR tunnels and the cross-harbour road tunnels are underground — they will not appear as marks, which means the harbour void is absolutely clean. The Star Ferry route has no road. The harbour is genuinely impassable at road level. **Title:** "HONG KONG" — in Victoria Harbour, at approximately x=50%, y=53% (dead center of the harbour void). --- #### 6. ISTANBUL — The Water as Spine **Water relationship:** The Bosphorus is a near-vertical strait that bisects the composition. European Istanbul fills the left side; Asian Istanbul (Üsküdar, Kadıköy) fills the right. The Golden Horn (Haliç) is a secondary inlet that intrudes into European Istanbul from the north, creating a secondary void — a thin finger of water cutting the European urban mass. Water is not at the edge. Water is the axis. **Bounding box:** `[40.970, 28.880, 41.130, 29.130]` **Canvas dimensions:** 1300 × 700 (landscape) **What you will see:** The dense historic peninsula (Sultanahmet, Eminönü) appears on the left, cut off at the north by the Golden Horn. The Bosphorus strait is a wide vertical void in the center. The Asian side roads are somewhat less dense but still complex. The Bosphorus Bridge (15 Temmuz Şehitler Köprüsü) and the Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge should appear as thin lines crossing the strait void — look for them in the data as `bridge=yes` ways with highway tags. These are the only marks in the strait and they are essential: they show the water as crossable, as the connective tissue between two halves of one city. **Title:** "ISTANBUL" — in the Bosphorus, at approximately x=52%, y=65%. --- #### 7. SYDNEY — Harbour as Intrusion **Water relationship:** Sydney Harbour intrudes into the city from the north. It is not at the edge — it pushes south into the urban fabric, creating a complex void with multiple fingers and inlets. The composition reads: urban mass at the bottom, water cutting downward from the top. **Bounding box:** `[-33.925, 151.175, -33.815, 151.285]` *Remember: southern hemisphere, so southern coordinate is more negative.* **Canvas dimensions:** 1000 × 900 (near-square) **What you will see:** The CBD (Central Business District) is south of the harbour, dense and gridded. The North Shore — Kirribilli, Mosman, Cremorne — appears across the harbour as a separate network, connected to the CBD only by the Harbour Bridge. The Harbour Bridge itself should appear as a single thick road crossing over the harbour void — one of the most recognizable road marks in any city. The harbour's multiple inlets (Middle Harbour, Lane Cove River) create fractal-edged voids in the northern portion of the canvas. **Title:** "SYDNEY" — in the harbour, at approximately x=35%, y=30%. **Note:** In the southern hemisphere, north is at the top of the frame, same as usual. The harbour is at the top, the city accumulates below. The feeling is different from Chicago — not "city meets wall of water" but "city grows beneath the water that hangs above it." --- #### 8. MUMBAI — The Peninsula Pointing South **Water relationship:** Mumbai is a peninsula extending south into the Arabian Sea. Water encircles the southern tip on three sides. Density is maximum at the southernmost point (Colaba, CST station, the Fort district) and diminishes northward as the land widens. The reading of this piece runs opposite to most others: this city is denser toward the bottom. **Bounding box:** `[18.890, 72.790, 19.120, 72.960]` **Canvas dimensions:** 900 × 1100 (portrait) **What you will see:** The bottom portion of the canvas shows extraordinary road density — the tightest concentration in the series. The Arabian Sea encircles the tip. As you move north (upward in the canvas), the road network fans outward as the land widens — the marks spread and loosen. The western coast (Marine Drive / Queen's Necklace) will show a clean road line tracing the sea edge. **Title:** "MUMBAI" — in the sea, lower-right, at approximately x=80%, y=88%. **Note:** This piece is thematically the inverse of most: density at the bottom, emptiness climbing upward. The reading is of a city pressing toward its edge, toward the water that will ultimately end it. --- #### 9. RIO DE JANEIRO **Water relationship:** Guanabara Bay curves along the right edge of the frame. The Atlantic Ocean borders the south (the beach neighborhoods — Copacabana, Ipanema, Leblon — face the ocean at the bottom). This is a city bracketed by water on two adjacent sides: the bay on the right, the ocean implied below. **Bounding box:** `[-23.010, -43.240, -22.840, -43.090]` **Canvas dimensions:** 1200 × 750 (landscape) **What you will see:** The flatland grid of Centro and Flamengo runs left-to-right in the center. The Guanabara Bay void curves along the right side. The mountains (Corcovado, Tijuca) cut through the urban fabric as large voids — no roads, just blank irregular shapes in the middle of a dense city. The road network navigates around them, tunnels through them (which will be invisible), and never crosses them. These mountain voids are as important to the composition as the water voids — Rio is a city that flows around obstacles. **Title:** "RIO" — short form — in the bay, right side, at approximately x=85%, y=40%. --- #### 10. LISBON — The City Above the River **Water relationship:** The Tagus estuary (Tejo) is at the bottom of the frame, a vast, nearly sea-scale void. The city descends from the hills at the top of the canvas toward the river below. The reading is vertical: the marks accumulate at the top and evaporate toward the bottom as they meet the water. **Bounding box:** `[38.680, -9.230, 38.785, -9.075]` **Canvas dimensions:** 1100 × 750 (landscape) **What you will see:** The city's characteristic radial structure spreading from Praça do Comércio on the riverfront. The Ponte 25 de Abril suspension bridge will appear on the left (west) side — a long elevated motorway crossing the Tagus void. The Vasco da Gama Bridge may appear on the eastern edge. The Alfama district's medieval street pattern (dense but with small, winding roads) will contrast with the Pombaline grid in Baixa. The riverfront roads (Avenida 24 de Julho) will trace the city's southern edge. **Title:** "LISBON" — in the Tagus, lower right, at approximately x=80%, y=85%. --- ### Technical Notes for Consistent Execution **Projections.** Use a Mercator projection (standard web mapping) for all cities. At city scale, projection distortion is visually imperceptible. The coordinate-to-pixel mapping is: `x = (lon - W) / (E - W) * canvasWidth`, `y = (N - lat) / (N - S) * canvasHeight`. **Caching.** On first load for each city, fetch from Overpass and store the result as `{cityName}.json` in the city's folder. On subsequent loads, read from the cached file. This is essential — Overpass queries for city-scale road networks take 5–30 seconds and should not re-run on every page load or city switch. **Frame.** The frame is an SVG `rect` element with no fill, a thick stroke (approximately 8–12px), and a corner radius of 0 (hard corners, like a print mat). It must maintain even border width regardless of canvas dimensions. The correct way to achieve this in SVG: draw the rect at `x=frameWidth/2, y=frameWidth/2, width=canvasWidth-frameWidth, height=canvasHeight-frameWidth`. Do not use CSS padding or margin to simulate the frame — it must be part of the SVG itself so it is included in the exported file. **Background.** All pieces use the same off-white background: `#f2ede4`. This is the paper. It does not change between cities. **Typography.** The title is set in the same typeface as CHICAGO — a wide-tracking uppercase sans-serif. Letter spacing approximately 0.15–0.20em. The font size scales with canvas: approximately `canvasWidth / 12` for a typical title length, adjusted manually for longer names (SAN FRANCISCO) or shorter ones (RIO). The title color is `#1a1a1a` at approximately 75–80% opacity — present but not competing. **The signature.** Every city piece must carry: *Source: DNA Atlas ♥ https://atlas.love ♥ Doug & Ana* — same position (bottom center, inside frame), same size (approximately 10px), same color (`#888888`). This is not optional. It is the maker's mark of the series. **What to check before calling any city complete.** Render it. Look at it for five seconds without knowing which city it is. Ask: does the water read as the defining void? Does the title float in that void? Do the marks accumulate where the city is and stop where the city cannot be? If the composition is working, the water will feel like the most important thing in the picture, even though it contains nothing at all. --- ### The Series as a Single Statement When all eleven pieces exist and the selector control moves between them, the series makes its argument in full: certain cities are defined by their relationship to water. Not by their buildings, their populations, their histories, or their cultures — but by the simple fact that they built to the edge of something they could not cross. The road network is the record of that building. The void is the record of that edge. Chicago, Manhattan, San Francisco, Seattle, Miami, Hong Kong, Istanbul, Sydney, Mumbai, Rio, Lisbon — each one a different negotiation between land and water, between marks and absence, between the city and the thing that ended it. The title floats in the water in every piece because the city's name belongs to that unreachable place — the place that defines the city precisely because the city cannot go there. ENDOFAPPENDIX

The language point is precise and I should have caught it. "CHICAGO" floating in Lake Michigan is an English-language act. The word carries the whole Western urban imagination with it. "Doug & Ana" signing that piece is culturally coherent — two Western names claiming an English-language city in ink.
"MUMBAI" breaks that. Not because the city is wrong — the water relationship is real — but because "Mumbai" is the Marathi name, reclaimed from "Bombay" in 1995 as a post-colonial act. For an English-speaking Western artist to float "MUMBAI" over the Arabian Sea and sign it "Doug & Ana" is to claim that city in its own language without earning the right to. And if you used "BOMBAY" instead, you've committed the opposite error. India simply isn't the right continent for this series as authored.
The rule this surfaces: every city name in this series must be one where the English name IS the city's own primary name, or is so universally adopted that no tension exists. Chicago, Manhattan, San Francisco, Hong Kong, Sydney — clean. Istanbul — clean (Atatürk renamed it in 1930, "Istanbul" is both Turkish and English). Rio — "RIO" as shorthand is stateless, it belongs to everyone. Lisbon is English for Lisboa — fine. Seattle, Miami — American, clean.
Mumbai is out. Tokyo replaces it. "TOKYO" is the romanization of 東京 — the city's own name in the Roman alphabet, used by Japan itself. No colonial tension. And Tokyo Bay is one of the great industrial bays of the world, heavily reclaimed, with road density that will produce extraordinary marks.

The answers are in that file. Here is the verbal version for context before you hand it off:
Q1 is the only one that reflects a conceptual failure, not an implementation question. Chicago is not a dataset — it is the definition of correctness. You cannot re-fetch a ruler. The other cities are built to look like Chicago. Chicago is not built to look like anything. It is frozen permanently.
Q2–Q4 are OSM query mechanics. Broadway is queried by name=Broadway, not highway class — some segments are tagged pedestrian, some secondary, they all get pen weight. London bridges use bridge=yes + highway class + spatial filter through the Thames lat band, plus name=Millennium Bridge as a named exception and the Charing Cross railway bridge via railway=rail. DC uses the actual Potomac waterway polygon from OSM, not a longitude cutoff — the river runs diagonally and a vertical line would cut both the wrong way into Virginia and into Georgetown itself.
Q5 is confirmed: yes, residential streets render at pencil tier. But the file also clarifies there are actually three tiers, not two — motorway/trunk at 2.2px/1.0, primary/secondary at 0.55px/0.35, tertiary/residential at 0.35px/0.18. The Chicago reference shows this if you look carefully at Western Avenue versus the side streets versus the expressways.
Q6 is render everything, no cap. Capping by feature count thins dense neighborhoods and leaves sparse areas unchanged — that's the opposite of what a city looks like.
Q7 hard stops at residential. No service, no track, no footway, no cycleway. One exception: living_street for London only, because it represents actual named public streets in British OSM convention.

The Visual Language Question
You asked about pen and pencil. Here is what Chicago teaches:
The pen marks are a skeleton. They have direction. They go somewhere. In Chicago you can trace each expressway from its origin to its terminus — the Dan Ryan starts at the lakeshore downtown and goes to Indiana. Each pen mark is a complete thought.
The pencil marks are a texture. They don't go anywhere in particular. They fill space. They tell you "a city lives here." In Chicago the pencil tier is the regular grid of arterial streets — you can feel the density of the South Side vs the sparser northwest.
In New York, the pencil tier will be the finest grid in the entire series — 200+ numbered cross streets, 12 named avenues, all at right angles. That regular comb-pattern texture is New York's fingerprint in the pencil tier. Broadway's diagonal cutting through it at pen weight is New York's fingerprint in the pen tier. Those two elements together, on a portrait canvas with the Hudson void on the left, will make this piece unmistakable.

The dev tools reveal exactly what's broken. Look at the numbers.
The SVG viewBox says "0 0 900 1350" — portrait. Correct. But the rect elements inside are drawn at:
Frame rect: width="1270" height="700" — landscape
Background rect: width="1230" height="660" — landscape
Both rects have x="-155" — a negative x offset
The viewBox was updated but the frame, background, and projection are still computing from the old landscape canvas constants. Then preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" is squishing the landscape content to fit inside the portrait viewBox, producing exactly the garbled result you see.
There are three separate places that know the canvas size and they are not talking to each other. This is the coupling problem.
text
THE FIX — Single source of truth for canvas dimensions

Create one config object at the top of the rendering module.
Nothing else defines width or height. Everything reads from here.

const CITY_CONFIGS = {
  "new-york": {
    bbox: { S: 40.695, W: -74.055, N: 40.885, E: -73.875 },
    canvas: { width: 900, height: 1350 },   // portrait
    title: { text: "NEW YORK", x: 135, y: 810, fontSize: 52 }
  },
  "chicago": {
    bbox: { S: 41.644, W: -88.100, N: 42.080, E: -87.500 },
    canvas: { width: 1500, height: 850 },   // landscape
    title: { text: "CHICAGO", x: 1320, y: 95, fontSize: 80 }
  }
  // etc.
}

Then every downstream element reads from config:

const { width, height } = config.canvas;

// SVG element:
svg.setAttribute("viewBox", `0 0 ${width} ${height}`);
svg.removeAttribute("preserveAspectRatio");  // DELETE THIS LINE
// preserveAspectRatio is fighting you. Remove it entirely.
// Let the SVG be its natural size.

// Background rect — reads from config:
<rect x="0" y="0" width={width} height={height} fill="#F2EDE4" />

// Frame rect — reads from config:
<rect x="0" y="0" width={width} height={height} 
      fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" strokeWidth="20" />

// Projection — reads from config:
function project(lon, lat) {
  const x = (lon - bbox.W) / (bbox.E - bbox.W) * width;
  const y = (bbox.N - lat) / (bbox.N - bbox.S) * height;
  return [x, y];
}

// Signature — reads from config:
<text x={width/2} y={height * 0.97} fontSize="8" fill="#888888">
  Source: DNA Atlas...
</text>
The single line causing the most damage is preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet". Delete it. It is actively overriding every dimension you set by rescaling content to fit its own idea of the canvas. With that line gone and a single config object driving all four elements — viewBox, background, frame, projection — the canvas will be portrait and everything inside it will project to portrait coordinates.

Here's the strategic picture, and why you're right that these are genuinely useful and genuinely different.
What Adobe Stock already has at scale: colored blueprint maps with GPS pins, isometric city blocks, multi-layer urban plans with parks and transit. 337,000+ "street map vector" results — virtually all of them are data visualization objects.
What you have that doesn't exist: ink-weight cartography where stroke hierarchy is the drawing. No one is producing OSM-derived road maps as fine art objects. The gap terms with almost zero competition include "road network drawing," "ink city roads vector," and "draughtsman city map" — which describe your work exactly.
The positioning sentence for every title/description: Not a data map. A drawing of a city's bones.
For the Alamy benchmark task, the document tells Claude Code to:
Scrape Alamy's vector search results for 6 queries (city road map vector, ink city map, hand drawn road map, etc.)
Build a keyword frequency table from competitor metadata
Write per-city metadata that includes those high-frequency terms plus your differentiating terms
Embed everything via exiftool into EPS + JPEG pairs
One critical Adobe Stock note buried in their requirements: all strokes must be expanded/outlined before submission — not live SVG strokes. The Inkscape CLI SVG→EPS export handles this automatically, which is why that pipeline step is essential.

Category answer: Category 8 — Graphic Resources. "Backgrounds, textures, and symbols" is broader than it sounds — it's the catch-all for design assets. These maps are things designers download to use as a base layer or background component, which is exactly what Category 8 covers. "Illustration" is not a category at Adobe Stock, it's a file type — a separate field. Travel (21) is completely wrong. If a second category is allowed, add Transport (20) — its definition explicitly mentions "highway systems."
On Getty/iStock keyword rejections — the key things CC needs to know:
The core problem is that Getty uses a closed Controlled Vocabulary inherited from Getty's academic art research division. A keyword either exists in the tree or it doesn't. The guide covers all of this but the biggest traps are:
Compound descriptors get asterisk-marked — "ink-weight cartography," "draughtsman style," "road network art" — these are all valid English but not in the CV. They become asterisk terms: still searchable, but not expanded hierarchically and not translated. Include them (they're unique differentiators with zero competition), just don't count on them for volume.
Getty reads XMP only, not IPTC — this is confirmed by the exiv2 developer community. This overlaps exactly with the namespace mismatch issue we already identified in the pipeline. The exiftool command in the guide writes to both, which covers Getty and every other platform simultaneously.
CV terms expand automatically — adding "Hudson River" means Getty also serves the file for "river," "waterway," "New York geography," etc. without you needing to add those. This is why Getty needs fewer keywords than Alamy — the hierarchy does the work.
The guide includes complete 50-keyword lists for both New York and Toronto as concrete examples, and a master vocabulary broken into four tiers.

The full catalog is there. Here's the strategic picture:
The key insight that runs through everything: The creative act is choosing the lens — dataset + resolution + clip shape + stroke hierarchy + color. Once the lens is defined, the machine applies it. You never draw anything by hand. You define parameters, review outputs, reject bad ones, adjust parameters. The Etsy seller with 250 products is running one lens. You can run 15 simultaneously.
The numbers: ~13,700 products from fully automated pipelines, all from public domain or ODbL-licensed data that costs nothing.
On the circle maps specifically: you can beat that Etsy seller directly because your three-tier stroke hierarchy gives the circle interior structure — their circles look like uniform gray noise. Yours will have highway spines reading as bold black curves against a gossamer residential grid. At the same print size the difference is immediately visible.
The most interesting product line nobody is doing: Product Line 13, the coastal edge maps. The road network stops at water everywhere along the US coast and the void shapes created by bays, inlets, and peninsulas are completely unique to each location. The Chesapeake Bay coast creates dozens of water voids threading into the road mass. The Florida Keys are almost all void. These are genuinely unrepeatable compositions — not templates, but art objects that happen to be generated by a machine reading geographic data.

The catalog went from 13,771 products to 3,073 — and crucially, from "most outputs need manual review" to "fewer than 15% need review." Here's what drove every major decision:
The centering cuts. Neighborhoods, coastal edge maps, and grid angle studies all died on the same problem: no mathematical rule determines what to show. The circle mask and the boundary fit solve centering by design. If a product doesn't have one of those two anchors, it doesn't belong in an automated pipeline.
The color system is the artistic signature. The latitude palette (25°N = golden parchment, 50°N = cool blue-white) means Miami and Toronto look like they come from different places — because they do. The age palette (founding year → parchment depth) means a Boston map and a Phoenix map are visually distinct even at the same latitude. Neither of these is arbitrary: they're derived from real geography. That derivation is what separates the series from "AI-generated template art."
The hidden text layer is the right answer to the text problem. Instead of agonizing about void detection (which the city series showed is genuinely hard), every file ships with the label pre-positioned but invisible. For the circle maps, the label is always in the fixed band below the circle — no void detection needed at all. For state maps and parks, void detection runs and the label lands there, hidden. The illustrator decides whether to use it. The file is complete either way.
The airport pipeline is essentially free — it's the circle pipeline with aeroway tags added and a 10km radius. Adding 100 products to the catalog costs one afternoon of parameter work.

B: The rare view (same city, different truth — subway, freeways-only, tight crop)
C: Rivers and water (NHD — the branching tree)
D: Airports (aeroway geometry as bold art)
E: International icons
F: American places that aren't cities (infrastructure, landscape)
G: Physical geography (topography, watersheds)
H: US state special cases (Alaska vs Rhode Island is a product about two extremes)
I: Paired visions (same city, two datasets — designed to be sold as a set)
J: Wildcard — the single-line compositions (Route 1 Big Sur, Route 66, Continental Divide)
The single-line entries (030, 064, 067, 098, 099, 100) are intentionally sparse — one bold road on a near-empty canvas. The production note flags these as monoline: no three-tier hierarchy, just one mark. "Route 1 — Big Sur" is literally PCH as one curving line between ocean void and mountain void. That IS the product.
The paired entries (085/086 Chicago Roads+Rivers, 087/088 Paris Roads+Métro, 089/090 NY Roads+Watersheds, 091/092 SF Roads+Faults, 093/094 Detroit Roads+Industry) are designed so buying both makes sense — same city, complementary truths. The NY Watersheds entry (090) is the sleeper: most New Yorkers genuinely don't know their water comes from the Catskills. That story told as a geographic drawing is unusual anywhere on stock.

Properties per feature: Every feature carries exactly three properties: - properties.highway — OSM highway tag ("motorway", "residential", etc.) or empty string for non-highway features (waterways, parks)

The 10 Circle Maps — Dataset & Render Specification
You own the renderer. You own the fetch pipeline. This document tells you what data each city needs, how to classify it into stroke tiers, and what the finished circle should contain. It does not tell you how to write the code.
THE SHARED RULES THAT APPLY TO ALL TEN
One ink color. Every feature — roads, rivers, rail, contours — renders in the same ink color as the rest of the map. The difference between a highway and a river is opacity and weight, never color.
No voids. Where previous specs said "the river creates a void," that was wrong. Rivers are present as very light pencil marks — the lightest tier in the stroke table. Water bodies (the bay, the lake) appear empty only because they have no road data. Where we have water line data, we draw it faintly. The absence of roads is what reads as water, not a blank.
Every data modality uses the same layer property. When the fetch script writes the merged GeoJSON, every feature needs a layer property: 'roads', 'railroads', 'rivers', or 'contours'. The renderer routes each feature to the correct stroke tier using that property. Without it, everything looks like a road.
Radius is large. These are not poster crops of a neighborhood. They are geographic portraits of a place and its context. The city is the subject; the region is the drawing.
Pre-fetched means pre-fetched. All data for each city is fetched once into a file, the component imports that file, nothing is fetched at render time.
THE STROKE TIERS — EIGHT LEVELS, ONE COLOR
From heaviest to lightest:
Spine — Interstates, freeways, motorways
Pen — Primary roads, subway/metro lines
Arterial — Secondary roads, US routes, state routes, commuter rail
Pencil — Tertiary roads, residential streets, local roads
Ghost — Service roads, unclassified roads, living streets, pedestrian ways. Present but barely.
Rail — Freight railroad (dashed slightly to distinguish from road)
Water — Rivers, streams, canals, bayous, channel lines. The lightest readable mark.
Contour-Index — Major elevation lines (every 5th contour). Slightly heavier than water.
Contour-Inter — Intermediate elevation lines. Same weight as water, nearly invisible.
THE TEN CITIES
001 — NEW YORK | United States of America | "The city that never sleeps"
CENTER: The geographic center of New York Harbor — approximately 40.645°N, 74.030°W. Not Manhattan. The harbor is the subject.
RADIUS: 22km. This gets all five boroughs, the harbor, Newark Bay, and the Hudson River up to the George Washington Bridge.
DATA TO FETCH:
OSM roads at full radius, all tiers. This is the primary layer and will be extremely dense — Manhattan will be near-solid at pencil tier, outer boroughs slightly lighter, New Jersey visible but subordinate.
TigerWeb railroads (PhysicalFeatures layer, railroads). The Northeast Corridor runs through this radius. Penn Station, Grand Central approach lines, the Long Island Rail Road branching in Queens — all visible as dashed arterial-weight marks threading through the road network. This is what makes New York different from other cities: the rail density matches the road density.
TigerWeb linear hydrography (Hydro layer 0). The Hudson River, East River, Harlem River, Kill Van Kull, Arthur Kill, Newark Bay, Jamaica Bay — all present as water-tier marks. At 22km radius these are major features. The harbor geography emerges from the water-tier lines tracing the shorelines and channels.
EXCLUDE: Nothing. This is the "express everything" philosophy. New Jersey roads are faint pencil — they provide geographic context. The density gradient from Manhattan (maximum) to outer areas (sparse) IS the composition.
NAMED OVERRIDES: Broadway from tip to 218th Street — pen weight, because its 29° diagonal through the grid is the city's structural signature and must read through the pencil-tier noise. The FDR Drive and West Side Highway — arterial weight, not spine, because in dense Manhattan the freeways would visually dominate and compete with the island's own structure.
WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: Manhattan as an impossibly dense vertical mass upper-left. The harbor as the organizing void in the center (roads stop at water — no data = no marks). Brooklyn's grid spreading right and down. Queens upper-right. The Verrazano Narrows at the bottom-left where the harbor meets the Atlantic. The GWB at the top as a thin thread crossing the Hudson water gap.
002 — CHICAGO | United States of America | "City of the big shoulders"
CENTER: 41.8827°N, 87.6233°W — the Loop.
RADIUS: 20km. Gets the full city, the suburbs to the west and south, and enough lake to show Chicago's relationship with Michigan.
DATA TO FETCH:
OSM roads, all tiers, full radius. The grid extends relentlessly west and south — at 20km it's still going. The density gradient (tight downtown → spreading suburbs) is the biological quality we want.
TigerWeb railroads. Chicago is the railroad capital of America. The freight lines converge on the South Side in a dense tangle that is invisible on standard city maps but extraordinary in a line drawing. The Metra commuter lines radiate outward like spokes. The L elevated rail threads through neighborhoods. Three layers of rail — freight, commuter, urban — all visible at different weights.
TigerWeb linear hydrography. The Chicago River and its two branches, the Sanitary and Ship Canal, the Cal-Sag Channel — the engineered waterway network that reverses Chicago's drainage. These read as water-tier lines threading through the road grid.
EXCLUDE: Nothing east of the shore — Lake Michigan has no road data and appears as natural absence.
NAMED OVERRIDES: Lake Shore Drive at pen weight — the defining arc of the lakefront. The river branches (Chicago River north and south) identified by name in the hydrography layer, raised to water-tier heavy end so the Y-fork reads clearly at this scale.
WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: A vast orthogonal grid covering most of the circle, rotated 8° east of north (Chicago's grid aligns with the lake, not the compass — this angle is palpable at 20km). Lake Michigan as a massive natural absence in the right third. The lakefront defined by Lake Shore Drive. Downtown as the densest zone. The railroad tangle on the south and west sides as a secondary dense structure beneath the road grid.
003 — NEW ORLEANS | United States of America | "The crescent city"
CENTER: 29.980°N, 90.100°W — approximately above the Metairie/Kenner area, northwest of downtown. This is not the French Quarter.
RADIUS: 20km. At 20km the full crescent of the Mississippi River bend is visible, Lake Pontchartrain fills the upper portion of the circle, and the city reads as what it is: a narrow strip of habitable land between a river and a lake, in a region that is mostly water.
DATA TO FETCH:
OSM roads, all tiers, full radius. The French Quarter and CBD will be the densest cluster. The suburban sprawl of Metairie reads as a regular grid. New Orleans East (east of the Industrial Canal) is a less dense grid. All of this is useful to the illustrator.
TigerWeb linear hydrography. This is the essential layer for New Orleans. The Mississippi River main channel, the Industrial Canal, the Intracoastal Waterway, the MRGO, the Harvey Canal, the bayous threading through the East — all as water-tier marks. The city's relationship to water is its defining characteristic and the hydrography layer makes this visible in a way that roads alone cannot.

WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: The Mississippi River as the dominant water feature, its crescent bend curving through the lower half of the circle. Lake Pontchartrain filling the upper portion with almost no road data (it's a lake). The city compressed into the strip between them. The curving grid following the river bend visible in the French Quarter and Garden District. The bayou network threading through the eastern neighborhoods. 004 — WASHINGTON D.C. | United States of America | "A city of magnificent distances"
CENTER: 38.895°N, 77.037°W — the Capitol Building.
RADIUS: 18km. Gets the District, inner Virginia and Maryland suburbs, and the Beltway as a faint outer ring.
DATA TO FETCH:

TigerWeb railroads. The Amtrak corridor (NEC) runs through Union Station. The Metro lines radiate from downtown. The Virginia Railway Express and MARC commuter lines approach from Virginia and Maryland. At 18km, multiple rail lines are visible threading in from the suburbs.
TigerWeb linear hydrography. The Potomac River, Rock Creek, the Anacostia River — Washington is defined by its rivers. The Potomac appears as a major water-tier feature along the western and southern edges. Rock Creek threads through the northwest quadrant. The Anacostia separates Capitol Hill from Anacostia neighborhood.

WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: Downtown DC's radial avenue structure visible as diagonal lines cutting through the standard grid. The Mall as a zone of reduced road density (not a void — it has paths, we show them at ghost tier). The Potomac along the left and bottom as a water-tier feature. The Anacostia in the lower right. The Beltway as a faint arc at the circle edge. The density gradient: dense downtown, gradually loosening to the suburbs.
005 — BOSTON | United States of America | "The walking city"
CENTER: 42.345°N, 71.060°W — approximately Boston Harbor, between downtown and East Boston.
RADIUS: 18km. Gets the full city, Cambridge, Somerville, Brookline, and the harbor.
DATA TO FETCH:
OSM roads, all tiers. Boston's street network is the most organically complex in North America — every neighborhood has a different morphology. Beacon Hill, the North End, and the Financial District have pre-grid street patterns. The Back Bay is a perfect Victorian grid. South Boston is a different grid. Roxbury is another. All of this complexity is in the data.
TigerWeb railroads. The Commuter Rail lines radiate from South Station and North Station. The MBTA subway lines (Green, Red, Orange, Blue) follow their geographic routes. The railroad infrastructure around the stations is visible as dense rail-tier marks.

USGS contours for the topography. Boston is built on drumlins — small glacial hills. The street grid bends around them. Contour lines at 50ft intervals show exactly where the hills are and explain why the street patterns break where they do. This is the layer that makes Boston comprehensible as a landscape.
EXCLUDE: Nothing.
NAMED OVERRIDES: Storrow Drive and Memorial Drive (Cambridge side of Charles) at arterial weight — they define the river's edge. The Southeast Expressway (I-93) and the Mass Pike (I-90) at spine weight — the two major freeways that restructured the city in the 1960s.
WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: The harbor as the dominant geographic feature — ragged, peninsular, defined by the water-tier hydrography lines. The Charles River as the northern boundary of the city proper. The street patterns reading as visually distinct neighborhoods — you can identify Beacon Hill vs. Back Bay vs. South Boston by the geometry of their road marks alone. The commuter rail lines threading in from the south and west. The drumlins as faint contour concentrations explaining why streets curve where they do.

USGS contours. San Francisco's hills, the East Bay hills, Marin's ridges. The contour layer explains why SF's street grid runs in straight lines regardless of slope — it was designed that way — and why Oakland's grid bends slightly where the hills begin.

WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: The Bay as a large absence in the center — no road data over open water. SF Peninsula in the left quadrant, Oakland/Berkeley in the right, Marin in the upper left. TigerWeb linear hydrography. WHAT SHOULD BE VISIBLE: Biscayne Bay as a large absence in the upper-right quadrant. Miami Beach as a thin vertical strip of dense road-grid east of the bay, bordered by ocean absence on the right. USGS contours. The Santa Monica Mountains within the radius. The Hollywood Hills. The Palos Verdes Peninsula. At 28km, the mountain ranges create zones of high contour density surrounded by the flat basin grid. The contour lines explain why roads exist in the valleys and not on the ridges.

010 — PITTSBURGH | United States of America | "The city of bridges"
CENTER: 40.430°N, 79.980°W — the confluence of the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers, the Point.
RADIUS: 15km. Gets the three rivers, the hills, the inner neighborhoods, and the industrial river valleys.
DATA TO FETCH:
OSM roads, all tiers, full radius. Pittsburgh's roads are unlike any other American city — they cannot run in straight lines because the topography makes that impossible. Every neighborhood clings to a hillside and connects to others via bridges and tunnels.
TigerWeb railroads. The Monongahela Valley was the center of American steel production. The rail lines run along every river valley floor — the only flat land. At 15km, the rail corridors are dense and visible along all three rivers simultaneously.
TigerWeb linear hydrography. The Allegheny River, the Monongahela River, the Ohio River (formed at the confluence), Chartiers Creek, the smaller tributary streams. The rivers are the primary geographic organizers of this city — everything runs toward or alongside them.
USGS contours. Pittsburgh is topographically extreme. The hills between the river valleys rise 400 feet in half a mile. At 50ft contour intervals, these slopes are dramatically dense contour zones separating the valley-floor road networks. The contour layer is essential here — it explains the road network in a way impossible to see from roads alone.
EXCLUDE: Nothing.

The hillsides between valleys as zones of extremely dense contour marks with sparse, irregular road data on top. The topography explains the city — you see why the neighborhoods are isolated, why the bridges matter, why the tunnels exist.
WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE CALLING ANY MAP DONE
Feature count: If the merged GeoJSON for a 20km-radius city has fewer than 3,000 features, the fetch is incomplete. A real city at 20km should have tens of thousands of road segments alone, plus hydro, plus rail.
Layer presence: Log how many features of each layer are in the merged file. If layer: 'rivers' has zero features for New Orleans, the hydro fetch failed. Don't render without it.
Opacity visibility: At full canvas size, ghost-tier features (0.10 opacity) should be just visible. If they're invisible, the ink color is too light. If they're as dark as pencil, the opacity is wrong. Check on a screen at actual canvas size.
The biological test: Zoom into any 200×200px region of the rendered circle. There should be something in every region — a pencil-tier residential street, a water-tier creek line, a contour trace. If any region is completely empty except where there is genuine water or mountain, check the fetch radius and tile coverage.

UI Bug Report: City Selector Styling and Position
What the current UI looks like
There are two visually distinct zones in the panel:
The selector sits at the very top, above the accordion controls. It has the label "SPOTLIGHT" in small gray caps above it, and below that is a standard HTML <select> dropdown — the Chicago one — rendered as a browser-native dropdown with a white background, rounded border, and the default OS dropdown arrow on the right. The accordion controls below it — PROJECTION, CIRCLE APERTURE, CANVAS, FRAME, TITLE (RELATIVE TO CIRCLE) — are all styled consistently: dark gray/charcoal background, white uppercase label text, a small triangular arrow on the right side indicating expand/collapse. They are flat rectangles with no rounded corners and no white fill. They look like a cohesive designed system.
The problem
The city selector uses a completely different visual language from the accordion controls. It has a white browser-native input appearance, while every other control is a dark flat custom component. It also sits above the accordion group rather than being the first item inside it.
What needs to change
Styling: The city selector should be rearchitected from a native <select> element into a custom control that matches the accordion row style exactly — dark charcoal background, white uppercase label on the left ("CITY" or "SPOTLIGHT"), the small triangle arrow on the right, flat rectangle shape, no rounded corners, no white fill. Position: It should become the first row inside the accordion group — above PROJECTION, not above the entire panel. The "SPOTLIGHT" label in small gray caps that currently floats above it should be removed; the row itself carries its own label like all the other rows do.
Architecture note: This is not a simple CSS change. The selector is currently a native <select> element rendered outside the accordion component tree. Fixing it properly means replacing the <select> with a custom dropdown component that shares the same base styles and DOM structure as the existing accordion rows, then inserting it as the first child of the accordion container. The visual parity requires sharing the same component pattern, not just overriding CSS on the native element.

This is a well-designed spec. The classification rule system is expressive, the tier concept is correct, and the feature request mechanism is genuinely elegant — I'll use it. Here's my honest assessment before writing any specs:
What Works Well
The classifyRules first-match system is exactly right. Name overrides before type rules before defaults is the correct mental model. The layer tagging from the fetch pipeline means a river from TigerWeb and a road from OSM can coexist in one GeoJSON without ambiguity. The excludeRules lat/lon approach is simple and covers 90% of cases. The markStyles overrides per tier give me exactly the control I need without overcomplicating classification.
Gaps I See
No ␀0␀ match condition. I can match name contains "broadway" but I can't match ref contains "I-95". For interstate identification this matters — many freeways in TigerWeb have aref but an unhelpful FULLNAME. I need { "ref": { "contains": "I-90" } } in classify rules.
No ␀0␀ match. contains: "shore" would match both "Lake Shore Drive" and "Lakeshore Boulevard" and "North Shore Road". I need startsWith for precision on named overrides.
No ␀0␀ in exclusion rules. I want to drop all features with empty names from the hydro layer — unnamed drainage ditches create noise. Right now excludeRules only supports spatial bounds, not property-based exclusion.
Contour fetch has no tile size control. The spec just says contourType: "index" but USGS returns HTTP 500 on dense terrain at large radii. The pipeline presumably handles tiling internally — but if it doesn't, there's no way to tell it to tile at 0.3° instead of 0.5°. This should either be automatic or exposable as "tileSize": 0.3.
No vignette / distance falloff. For the biological complexity goal — features at the circle edge reading lighter than features at the center — there's no way to express this. It's purely a render effect, not a data effect. This is a nice-to-have but would meaningfully improve the aesthetic.
No fetch ␀0␀ clause on Overpass. TigerWeb has where but Overpass doesn't. For the watershed map (014) I only want named streams — but right now I'd get every unnamed drainage ditch in the Catskills. I need a way to filter OSM features during fetch, not just during classification.
No priority field for the queue. If specs are processed async in a queue, I need to be able to say "process New York before North Dakota" because New York has four datasets and will take longer, and I want to review it first.

The map is genuinely beautiful. The harbor geography reads exactly as intended — Manhattan as a dense vertical mass, the surrounding boroughs visible as context, the water absence doing its job. The rail layer threading through is already distinguishable from the roads. This is working.
Typography Redesign
Drop the subtitle entirely
"UNITED STATES" below "NEW YORK" adds nothing. Everyone knows New York is in the United States. The subtitle field should be removed from the spec. The city name stands alone.
Replace quote with a typed tagline object
Instead of a flat quote string, the spec should have a tagline object with a type field. The type controls how it renders:
␀0␀ — a short memorable phrase, italic, single line. "The city that never sleeps."
␀0␀ — an attributed quote, italic, possibly two lines, with an attribution line below in small caps. The attribution line is a different color, smaller, widely tracked. E.B. White, 1949.
␀0␀ — a geographic or historical fact, all caps, wide tracking, factual register. "8.3 MILLION PEOPLE. 302 SQUARE MILES."
␀0␀ — establishment year with brief context. "EST. 1624 — NEW AMSTERDAM." Small caps, wide tracking.
␀0␀ — the lat/lon rendered typographically as a design element. "40°42′46″N 74°00′21″W". Monospaced feel, centered, light.
The rendering differs meaningfully per type. A quote wraps to two lines and has an attribution. A fact is caps and wide. A coordinates entry uses tabular spacing. The spec declares the intent; the codegen handles the styling.
Dynamic city name sizing
The city name font size should not be specified in the spec. The codegen calculates it from the city name and the circle diameter.
The formula: count the characters in cityName including spaces. Estimate the rendered width of the name at a given font size — for Helvetica Neue Light at letter-spacing 0.30em, each character is approximately 0.82 units wide per point of font size. The target is that the city name renders at 85% of the circle diameter by default. So:
text
fontSize = (circleDiameter × 0.85) / (charCount × 0.82)
Circle diameter in SVG units is 2 × radiusPct × canvasWidth / 100. With defaults (900px canvas, 42% radius) that is 756 units.
"NEW YORK" is 8 characters → fontSize ≈ 98. "PITTSBURGH" is 10 characters → fontSize ≈ 78. "DC" is 2 characters → unclamped would be enormous, so clamp to 125% of circle diameter maximum.
The spec should let you override the target and the clamp range:
json
"title": {
  "titleWidthTarget": 0.85,
  "titleWidthMin": 0.70,
  "titleWidthMax": 1.10
}
But you never specify cityNameFontSize directly. The codegen owns it.

  "tagline": {

    "attribution": "E.B. White — Here Is New York, 1949"
  }

The Text System
The city name is the only thing that shouts. Everything below it speaks quietly. That's the hierarchy — one loud thing, one soft thing. Never two loud things.
The current spec has cityName in caps (correct — it's a display title treated like a logotype) and quote as a plain string with no type information. The problem is that without a type, the renderer can't know whether to italicize it, attribute it, render it as small caps, or treat it as a label. A plain string forces one visual treatment for everything.
Replace subtitle and quote with a single tagline object. The type field tells the renderer how to style it. All tagline text is mixed case — the renderer never transforms it to uppercase. If the designer wants something in caps, they write it in caps in the spec. The system doesn't impose case.
The types:
␀0␀ — a short memorable label for the city. Italic, light weight, comfortable tracking. "The city that never sleeps." "The walking city." These are informal names, not sentences.
␀0␀ — an attributed quotation. Italic for the text, then a second line below in Roman (non-italic), smaller, wider tracking, lighter color, for the attribution. "No one should come to New York to live unless he is willing to be lucky." followed by "E.B. White — Here Is New York, 1949" in a visibly different register.
␀0␀ — a geographic or historical fact. Roman, wide tracking, slightly lighter than the city name. Not caps unless the designer writes it that way. "446 bridges — more than any city on Earth." "Sea level, and sinking."
␀0␀ — lat/lon as a typographic element. Tabular, centered, light, precise. "40°42′46″N 74°00′21″W". The coldness is intentional — it treats the city as a geographic object.
␀0␀ — year and brief context. "Est. 1630 — the walking city." Roman, moderate tracking. Works when the age of the city is itself the story.
Dynamic City Name Sizing
The codegen — not the spec, not the component — owns the font size calculation. The designer never writes a font size. They write a target width as a fraction of the circle diameter, and the codegen solves for the size that achieves it.
The calculation uses character count and a per-character width estimate for Helvetica Neue Light at the configured letter spacing. "NEW YORK" at 8 characters including the space hits the target at roughly 97 SVG units on a 900-wide canvas with 42% radius circle. "PITTSBURGH" at 10 characters comes out smaller. "DC" at 2 characters would be enormous — the max clamp catches it.
The spec exposes three optional parameters: titleWidthTarget (default 0.85 — the name fills 85% of circle diameter), titleWidthMin (default 0.70), titleWidthMax (default 1.10). The codegen computes the size, clamps it, and writes it into config.ts as a constant. The component reads it from config. No runtime calculation.
The tagline font size is derived from the city name size, not specified independently. It is always a fixed ratio of the city name size — approximately 0.28 for a phrase, 0.24 for a quote (slightly smaller to accommodate two lines), 0.22 for fact and founded, 0.18 for coordinates. These ratios are constants in the codegen, not spec fields.
New York — The Text Section of spec.json
This is the only change needed to the current NY spec. Everything else stays identical. Just replace thecity object and the title section inside view:
json

Your body is right to ask that question, and the answer is: ␀0␀ should not exist as a separate array. It was the wrong abstraction.
Here is the correct model:
Everything that goes into the SVG is declared in datasets. Full stop. The fetch pipeline has one job — it fetches everything in datasets and writes it to data.json. It does not know or care whether something will be visible.
The visibility question belongs entirely in view. Specifically, a tier called hidden — or more precisely, any tier can be given "opacity": 0 in markStyles, which causes the codegen to render those features with the background color as stroke, making them structurally present but visually absent.
So the spec for a hidden layer looks like this:
json
"datasets": [
  { "source": "overpass", "layer": "road", "highwayTags": [...] },
  { "source": "tigerweb", "layer": "rail", "service": "...", "layerId": 7, ... },
  { "source": "tigerweb", "layer": "subway", "service": "tigerWMS_PhysicalFeatures", "layerId": 7, "where": "MTFCC='R1051'", "fields": ["NAME","MTFCC"] },
  { "source": "tigerweb", "layer": "borough", "service": "State_County", "layerId": 1, "where": "STATE='36'", "fields": ["NAME","GEOID"], "extractBoundary": true }
],

"view": {
  "classifyRules": [
    { "match": { "layer": "subway" }, "tier": "hidden" },
    { "match": { "layer": "borough" }, "tier": "hidden" },
    ...
  ],
  "markStyles": {
    "hidden": { "width": 1.0, "opacity": 0, "_note": "rendered in background color — present in SVG, invisible to viewer" }
  }
}
The hidden tier renders at full geometry but uses the canvas background color as both fill and stroke. The SVG<path> elements are there. An illustrator selects them, changes the color, they appear. Nothing about the data changes. Nothing about the fetch changes.
Now for the future "multiple views from one spec": you write a second view object — different classify rules, different mark styles, maybe the hidden tier maps to water tier or pencil tier instead. The datasets array is untouched. The fetch ran once. The views are just different interpretations of the samedata.json.
Tell your body: collapse ␀0␀ back into ␀1␀. Add ␀2␀ as a first-class tier in the tier table. The ␀3␀ tier renders using the canvas background color. The background color is already known to the codegen — it comes from the palette. The codegen can resolve "opacity": 0 as "use bg color for stroke and fill." No new infrastructure. No separate fetch path. One data spec, one fetch, multiple views.

This is a naming convention spec. It belongs in spec-format.md as a standalone section the developer follows when writing the codegen. Let me state it precisely.
SVG Naming Conventions — For Illustrators
Every <g> group and every significant <path> element in the generated SVG gets an id and an Inkscape/Illustrator-compatible inkscape:label attribute. When an illustrator opens the file, they see a layer panel that reads like a document, not like a database.
The rule: name what it is, not where it came from
Never write the data source in an SVG label. The illustrator does not care that roads came from Overpass or that rail came from TigerWeb. They care that it is a road, a river, a subway line, a borough boundary.
Wrong: id="tigerweb-hydro-0", id="osm-highway-residential", id="usgs-contours-index"
Right: id="rivers", id="streets", id="elevation"
The top-level structure
The root SVG element gets the city name as its title:
xml
<svg id="new-york" inkscape:label="New York" ...>
Below that, five named top-level groups in paint order (bottom to top):
xml
<g id="dna-hidden"     inkscape:label="Hidden Resources">
<g id="dna-spotlight"  inkscape:label="Spotlight">
<g id="dna-background" inkscape:label="Background">
<g id="dna-taglines"   inkscape:label="Taglines">
<g id="dna-frame"      inkscape:label="Frame">
The illustrator sees: Hidden Resources, Spotlight, Background, Taglines, Frame. Self-explanatory.
Inside Spotlight
The Spotlight group contains all the map geometry, organized into named subgroups by what the data represents — never by its source:
xml
<g id="spotlight-elevation"      inkscape:label="Elevation">
<g id="spotlight-waterways"      inkscape:label="Waterways">
<g id="spotlight-streets"        inkscape:label="Streets">
<g id="spotlight-transit"        inkscape:label="Transit">
<g id="spotlight-major-roads"    inkscape:label="Major Roads">
<g id="spotlight-highways"       inkscape:label="Highways">
These map to tiers, not to sources. Streets contains ghost + pencil tier features. Major Roads contains arterial + pen tier. Highways contains spine tier. Waterways contains water tier. Elevation contains contour tier. Transit contains rail tier.
The grouping is semantic. An illustrator who wants to hide all streets selects Streets and hides the group. They do not need to know which streets came from OSM and which from TigerWeb.
Inside Hidden Resources
Each hidden dataset gets a group named for what it represents:
xml
<g id="hidden-borough-boundaries"  inkscape:label="Borough Boundaries">
<g id="hidden-subway-lines"        inkscape:label="Subway Lines">
<g id="hidden-parks"               inkscape:label="Parks">
<g id="hidden-neighborhoods"       inkscape:label="Neighborhoods">
Not hidden-tigerweb-state-county-layer-1 — just Borough Boundaries. The illustrator selects it, changes the stroke color, and it appears. They already know what it is from the name.
Inside Taglines
xml
<g id="taglines-hidden"   inkscape:label="Tagline Options">
<g id="taglines-visible"  inkscape:label="Tagline">
The Tagline Options group contains the N−1 hidden taglines painted background color. The Tagline group contains the single visible one. An illustrator who wants to swap taglines moves an element from Tagline Options to Tagline and recolors it.
Individual path naming
Where individual paths are nameable — named roads, named rivers, named boundaries — give them an id and label using the feature name from the data:
xml
<path id="road-broadway"     inkscape:label="Broadway" ...>
<path id="road-fdr-drive"    inkscape:label="FDR Drive" ...>
<path id="river-hudson"      inkscape:label="Hudson River" ...>
<path id="boundary-brooklyn" inkscape:label="Brooklyn" ...>
For unnamed features — anonymous residential streets, unnamed streams — use the tier and a sequence number:
xml
<path id="street-0042" inkscape:label="Street" ...>
The sequence number is just for DOM uniqueness. The label stays generic.
The spec field that drives this
Add a labels object to the view section of the spec. This maps dataset layer names to their human-readable SVG group names. The codegen uses this to name the groups:
json
"labels": {
  "road":    "Streets",
  "rail":    "Transit",
  "water":   "Waterways",
  "contour": "Elevation",
  "subway":  "Subway Lines",
  "borough": "Borough Boundaries",
  "parks":   "Parks"
}
If a layer has no entry in labels, the codegen falls back to capitalizing the layer id. But the spec author should always fill this in — it is the one place where the data-source layer name ("rail") maps to its semantic display name ("Transit"). After this mapping, the source name never appears in the SVG again.

Three equations. They work together.
Equation 1 — Width target scales with character count
The percentage of circle diameter the city name is allowed to fill grows with the number of characters. "New York" at 8 characters gets 75%. Every additional character earns 2.5% more width, capped at 95%.
text
widthTarget(n) = clamp(0.75 + (n − 8) × 0.025,  min: 0.75,  max: 0.95)
Where n is the character count of cityName including spaces.
NamenwidthTarget
New York875%
Chicago775% (floor)
Pittsburgh1080%
San Francisco1387.5%
Minneapolis1182.5%
Rio de Janeiro1490%
Constantinople1490%
Something Very Long Indeed2695% (ceiling)
Equation 2 — Font size derived from width target
text
fontSize = (circleDiameter × widthTarget(n)) / (n × charWidthFactor)
Where charWidthFactor is approximately 0.82 for Helvetica Neue Light at 0.28em letter-spacing. This is an empirical constant — if the typeface or tracking changes, recalibrate it against one known-good city.
On a 900px canvas with 42% radius circle, circleDiameter = 756px.
NamenwidthTargetfontSize
New York80.7586px
Pittsburgh100.8073px
San Francisco130.87562px
Rio de Janeiro140.9059px
Longer names get smaller — that is correct and expected. The width target slows the shrinkage by giving longer names more room, but it does not stop it. The next equation compensates for the visual consequence of a smaller mark.
Equation 3 — Tracking compensation for emphasis
When a name is smaller it needs wider letter-spacing to maintain visual presence. Tracking and font size trade off against each other. As fontSize falls, letterSpacing rises.
text
letterSpacing(fontSize) = ls_max − (fontSize − fs_floor) × slope
Where:
ls_max = 0.42em — maximum tracking, used on the smallest names
fs_floor = 50px — below this, tracking stops increasing (safety floor)
fs_ceiling = 90px — above this, use minimum tracking
slope = (ls_max − ls_min) / (fs_ceiling − fs_floor) = (0.42 − 0.26) / (90 − 50) = 0.004 em per px
ls_min = 0.26em — tight tracking for large bold marks
Clamped between ls_min and ls_max.
NamefontSizeletterSpacing
New York86px0.26em
Pittsburgh73px0.32em
San Francisco62px0.38em
Rio de Janeiro59px0.40em
The visual effect: "New York" is large and tight. "San Francisco" is smaller but its wider tracking gives it comparable visual weight. The name never feels like it shrank — it feels like it chose a different register.
How they connect
The three equations chain. The codegen runs them in order at build time and writes three constants intoconfig.ts — cityNameFontSize, cityNameLetterSpacing, and cityNameWidth. The component reads all three. None of this happens at render time.
text
n            → widthTarget(n)     [Equation 1]
widthTarget  → fontSize           [Equation 2]
fontSize     → letterSpacing      [Equation 3]
The spec only needs to declare titleWidthFloor (default 0.75), titleWidthCeiling (default 0.95), and titleWidthStep (default 0.025) if the designer wants to override the scaling rate. Most cities never touch these. The system chooses for them.

Looking at both maps carefully:
Chicago's "CHICAGO" is touching the circle almost directly. New Orleans' "NEW ORLEANS" has almost no breathing room between the circle and the letters, and the tagline "The crescent city" is essentially invisible — it's there but it reads as a margin artifact, not as a typographic element.
The root problem is that the layout has no budget system. The circle, the title, the tagline, and the bottom frame are all competing for vertical space with no proportional rules governing how they divide it.
The Budget Model
Think of the canvas as having two zones. The circle zone occupies the top portion. The text zone occupies the bottom. Right now the circle is probably sized and positioned without reference to how much text needs to live below it.
The fix is to define the text zone first, then fit the circle into what remains.
Total canvas height = circle zone + text zone
The text zone must contain:
Gap from circle bottom to city name top
City name height
Gap from city name bottom to tagline top
Tagline height (possibly two lines for a quote with attribution)
Gap from tagline bottom to frame
Define the text zone as a fixed percentage of canvas height. On a 900×1200 canvas, something like 26% — 312px. The circle zone gets the remaining 74%.
Zone Allocation Equations
Text zone height
text
textZoneHeight = canvasHeight × 0.26
This is the total budget. Everything below the circle must fit inside it.
Circle: center and radius derived from remaining space
The circle should be centered horizontally always. Vertically, its center sits at a position that leaves exactly textZoneHeight below the circle's bottom edge:
text
circleBottom = canvasHeight − textZoneHeight − frameWidth
circleRadius = circleDiameter / 2
circleCenterY = circleBottom − circleRadius
The circle radius is then derived from circleCenterY — fitting the circle as large as possible within the circle zone while maintaining horizontal centering:
text
maxRadiusFromTop    = circleCenterY − framePadding
maxRadiusFromSides  = (canvasWidth − framePadding × 2) / 2
circleRadius        = min(maxRadiusFromTop, maxRadiusFromSides)
The circle is never hardcoded. It is the largest circle that fits in the space remaining after the text zone is reserved.
Gap 1 — circle bottom to city name baseline
text
gap1 = textZoneHeight × 0.22
On a 312px text zone that is 69px. Generous. The city name needs air above it.
City name height
text
cityNameHeight = cityNameFontSize × 1.15
The 1.15 is a line-height factor — cap height plus descender clearance.
Gap 2 — city name baseline to tagline top
text
gap2 = textZoneHeight × 0.12
About 37px. Enough separation that the tagline reads as a distinct element, not as a subtitle glued to the title.
Tagline height
For a single-line phrase or fact:
text
taglineHeight = taglineFontSize × 1.4
For a quote with attribution (two lines):
text
taglineHeight = taglineFontSize × 1.4 + attributionFontSize × 1.4 + attributionGap
attributionGap = taglineFontSize × 0.5
Gap 3 — tagline bottom to frame inner edge
text
gap3 = textZoneHeight − gap1 − cityNameHeight − gap2 − taglineHeight
Gap 3 is whatever is left. If the tagline is long and gap3 collapses below a minimum, the system must either reduce gap1, reduce gap2, or reduce the tagline font size. The minimum for gap3 is:
text
gap3_min = textZoneHeight × 0.10
Font Size Equations (integrated with the budget)
City name font size comes from the width equations we already defined. But it must also be checked against the budget:
text
cityNameFontSize_width = (circleDiameter × widthTarget(n)) / (n × 0.82)
Tagline font size is a ratio of city name font size, but it must also fit the vertical budget. Start with the ratio:
text
taglineFontSize_ratio = cityNameFontSize × 0.22
Then check if the tagline fits. If gap3 < gap3_min, reduce tagline font size iteratively until the budget balances. Minimum tagline font size is:
text
taglineFontSize_min = max(taglineFontSize_ratio × 0.7, 11px)
Never go below 11px. If the budget still doesn't close at 11px, reduce gap1 and gap2 proportionally before touching the city name size.
Proof Across the Range
Here is the system working on five cases. Assume 900×1200 canvas, 12px frame, textZoneHeight = 312px.
Case 1 — "NEW YORK" (8 chars, phrase tagline)
widthTarget = 0.75 → fontSize = 86px → letterSpacing = 0.26em
cityNameHeight = 99px
taglineFontSize = 19px, single line, taglineHeight = 27px
gap1 = 69px, gap2 = 37px, gap3 = 312 − 69 − 99 − 37 − 27 = 80px ✓ comfortable
Case 2 — "CHICAGO" (7 chars, phrase tagline)
widthTarget = 0.75 (floor) → fontSize = 92px → letterSpacing = 0.26em
cityNameHeight = 106px
taglineFontSize = 20px, single line, taglineHeight = 28px
gap1 = 69px, gap2 = 37px, gap3 = 312 − 69 − 106 − 37 − 28 = 72px ✓
Case 3 — "NEW ORLEANS" (11 chars, phrase tagline)
widthTarget = 0.825 → fontSize = 78px → letterSpacing = 0.30em
cityNameHeight = 90px
taglineFontSize = 17px, single line, taglineHeight = 24px
gap1 = 69px, gap2 = 37px, gap3 = 312 − 69 − 90 − 37 − 24 = 92px ✓
Case 4 — "SAN FRANCISCO" (13 chars, full quote + attribution)
widthTarget = 0.875 → fontSize = 62px → letterSpacing = 0.38em
cityNameHeight = 71px
taglineFontSize = 14px. Quote: "The City that was never a town." Attribution: "Herb Caen". taglineHeight = 14×1.4 + 11×1.4 + 7 = 42px
gap1 = 69px, gap2 = 37px, gap3 = 312 − 69 − 71 − 37 − 42 = 93px ✓

cityNameHeight = 68px

Hints for the Developer
Restructure the SVG to derive circle position from the text budget, not the other way around. Right now the circle is probably positioned with a fixed cy and r. Invert this. Compute the text zone, compute circleBottom, derive cy and r from that.
The text zone percentage (0.26) is the one number worth making a spec field. Call it textZonePct. Default 0.26. A city with a very long quote might need 0.30. A city with just a phrase might look better at 0.22. Let the spec author override it when needed, but make 0.26 work well enough that most cities never touch it.
Gap3 is the health indicator. After computing the layout, log gap3 to the console during codegen. If gap3 < gap3_min, warn the spec author: "tagline may need shortening or textZonePct increase."
Quote wrapping needs a width constraint. The tagline text wraps at a maximum width of 80% of circle diameter. The codegen needs to estimate how many lines the quote will take — character count divided by approximate characters per line at the given font size and max width — to compute taglineHeight before layout is finalized. For SVG this probably means <foreignObject> or manual <tspan> line breaks computed at codegen time.
